The house resumed, from Monday, June 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe, Port Arthur (for Mr. St. Laurent) for the second reading of Bill No. 256, to amend the Defence Production Act.
Mr. John Pallet! (Peel): Mr. Speaker, this bill, introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), to set up permanently the Department of Defence Production, and to establish permanently in the minister the powers presently contained in the act, and which is being introduced under the guise of a continuing emergency, underrates the intelligence, the integrity and the insight of the Canadian people. It does appear in some aspects, in view of the stubbornness which has been evidenced by the minister in the matter, that this measure is not a wolf in sheep's clothing, but rather the wolf itself. Having shed the sheep's clothing put around it in 1951 it now stands, with fangs bared, a serious threat to the basic and fundamental elements of democracy as we, and I think most Canadians, understand it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Defence Production Act
What manner of bill is this that is espoused by the government of this country, which for the time being is Liberal, and which Liberal creed is espoused from time to time as being a proponent of the principles of free enterprise? I have with me a copy of the mid-June edition of The Rural Scene, in which are some interesting definitions. Democracy, socialism, freedom, Liberal and Conservative have been defined as follows:
Democracy: Government of all the people within a jurisdiction, by all the people, and for all the people, all the time. A political means of safeguarding the inalienable, natural, rights of each person or minority. A legal system for the establishment and enforcement of law designed to create equality of opportunity, to impose equality of responsibility and to maintain democratic freedom.
Socialism: The political and economic expression of the fear of freedom. Compulsion is the socialistic means, usually sanctified by majorities, of vesting in the state the natural rights of all persons and minorities.
Freedom:	The exercise of inalienable,
natural, rights within a democracy.
Liberal: One who favors democratic reform and the abolition of privilege.
Conservative: One who seeks to enlarge [DOT]democratic good by the extension of tried institutions.
Can this bill be introduced by a Liberal :government? Continuity of thought and action, continuity of promise and production have never been outstanding elements in the liberal creed. However, the cardinal principle of free enterprise has rarely been subjugated to such violation by vacillation even by these masters of the art. One must conclude, therefore, one of two things: Either that under the pretence of continuing an integral element of democracy is concealed an effort to appease two parties in the country or that under such a pretence one party is attempting to assume permanent powers never before given by people, but rather forced or subverted from a people by similar devious measures.
Canada and Canadians, this is a crossroads! 1 would that we could hear Sir John A. and Sir Wilfrid at this moment.
Is it not fantastic that a nation which not only embraces but survives through a complete belief, understanding and practice of the principle of free enterprise should be thought so puerile that such an act of compulsion would be necessary? Our people are not only a nation adult in a physical and mechanical understanding of free enterprise, but also in its more far-reaching, tenacious, demanding, spiritual claims on our social conscience and collective soul. This government

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
can hardly regulate the heartbeats of the soul of a nation. What contempt this government must have for the people of Canada. Have not the people risen to the hour of need at all times? Has not the Prime Minister within the last few days in an interview with the press said he hopes it will never be necessary to have national service? National service affects a small portion of the population. This bill affects every portion of the working population. It is a complete reversal of his ideas with respect to conscription. Even in times of greatest emergency while there has been conscription for the armed services, there has never been conscription of farm, factory workers and stenographers.
By introducing this bill and in reading the words of the bill, this government says that it places more reliance on one minister than it does in the ability of the whole Canadian people to respond to a situation which would endanger the safety of the nation.

Mr. Pallet!: I am certainly pleased to hear that some of the members on the government side think I am reading this speech. I would certainly like to hear what they think of this Defence Production Act.
Is this government, or the members of it, prepared to come before this house and say who is the man who will administer this act? Will they say this is the man of the hour in whom we put out great trust? This is a man of infallible decisions. This man is wiser, more able, more far-seeing, more trustworthy, more conscientious than Canadians as a whole. Where is the man, if they say they have one? He is certainly not sitting on the present government benches, and I do not think anyone on this side of the house would have the temerity to suggest-

Mr. Pallet!: -that he is sitting here. If there is no such man or men, then why ask us to place powers on a permanent basis in the hands of an unknown quantity? There is a saying that power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely. What manner of man wants such powers? What type of man wants such powers?
During the discussion at the resolution stage of this bill, at page 2003 of Hansard, all members of the house understood that an understanding had been reached that consideration would be given to reviewing the permanent powers aspects of this bill. It was understood that consideration would result in the setting up of a permanent Department of Defence Production, but that the powers of the department would be subject to review within a reasonable period.
Defence Production Act I should point out at this time that the present powers under the act, passed in 1951, extend until 1956. In view of the general understanding that the bill, when finally introduced, would contain some definite dates for an opportunity to review the powers and would not ask for powers of a permanent nature, the resolution was supported, read the second time and concurred in.
I suppose the changes were considered, but I wonder what considerations were applied? From the type of defence of the bill offered by supporters of the government so far, and from the lack of explanation offered by the majority of the members on the government side, it would appear that the bill as presented does not have the support of the members on the government side that a measure of this kind ought to have. When it comes to the time of the vote, will government members put their party responsibilities before their responsibilities to Canada? I wonder if the Prime Minister would be prepared to say to government members that this is a free vote, or will they be asked to place in the hands of one man the power to walk into any plant, factory or farm in their riding and take it over?
It has been my experience when matters are coming up in the house which affect any part or any section of Canada to receive letters, briefs and submissions supporting the legislation as it is introduced or advocating that the legislation be opposed. These briefs come from associations of the better type, usually non-political. These briefs are valuable because no individual member of the house can formulate without some assistance an intelligent opinion on much of the legislation put through the house.
Someone with the support of this house has dared to so artificially and yet effectively subdue this magnificent manifestation of the feelings of our country that not just one but all of our nation's most influential, necessary organizations have not presented briefs on this debate. The presentation of briefs not only is customary but is of the greatest value in aiding the assessments made by this house of legislation. Assuredly the lack of briefs could hardly be accounted for by the indifference of these organizations. On the contrary, this debate is obviously of the utmost significance to them. But they are controlled by a reign of fear, a fear that is analogous to the fear inspired in an honest shopkeeper by the upper-echelon protection racketeer. Has the bludgeon, clothed scantily in an excessive majority, been at work?
Who is not producing at the present time in accordance with the contracts which have

Defence Production Act been made? No one has been named. If you read the white paper tabled by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) under the heading "equipment", you will find the following in paragraph 151:
During the first nine months of the fiscal year 1954-55,	101,900 contracts were placed by the
Department of Defence Production for defence equipment and stores, amounting to $747,967,000 in value.
Have the powers contained in this act aided in the production of all those contracts or in the placing of those contracts? Then with respect to naval equipment we find the following in paragraph 152:
No additional contracts have beeen placed for new naval vessels during the fiscal year 1954-55.
And in the same paragraph:
The destroyer escort program is unquestionably the most challenging of its kind ever carried out in this country. The over-all time of production compares favourably with that for similar projects in the United Kingdom and the United States.
And then paragraph 158 dealing with army equipment:
New equipment for the Canadian army was purchased to a total value of $95,270,000 during the past year. Most of this equipment was produced in Canada, but some was obtained from the United Kingdom or the United States.
Most of this equipment was produced in Canada. With respect to air force equipment, we find this at paragraph 163:
Production and delivery of the CF-100 Mk 4 is now well under way at Avro Aircraft Limited.
In paragraph 164:
Sabre production at Canadair Limited, Cartier, Quebec, is on schedule.
Nowhere in the white paper does the Minister of National Defence indicate that there have been any delays in production, but rather the tone of the white paper is to the contrary, and this bears out the original premise that Canadians as a whole are faithful and do not have to be bullied into doing that which they think is in the best interest of the country. People have only to read the white paper to see how well that premise is carried out according to the Minister of National Defence.
I well recall during the last war incidents when enemy ammunition was defective and we were told that the reason for this was that it was made by slave labour and that because we are a free people our production is better and more conscientious. This Defence Production Act was originally passed in 1951 when we were on a fringe of the new look in warfare and when the members of this house had not yet grasped the fact that, no matter what mechanical, chemical or biological advances are made, these are only elements to be used by us and form a small part of our general philosophy. In 1951, because there was a sudden expansion of [Mr. Pallett.l
things new, human minds at that time had grasped them as being part of something that was surmounting even our old principles and passed what they believed to be necessary legislation at that time. They forsook basic principles.
But everything must eventually come to its proper place, and these new developments have been put in their proper places. We have come to accept them as merely a part of our life and a part to be implemented for us. We are not to be subjugated to them. The fear of fantasy has passed and we now have a cold, stark realization that the fear of autocracy is here. How can there be autocracy in a democratic world? Read this act; see the unmitigated powers given to one minister. There can be no compromise on this bill as it presently stands.

Mr. Speaker, when, in 1951, the Defence Production Act was written into our statutes, it was understood that, by its very nature, it was to be of a temporary character and designed to meet a situation which was then considered to be critical. The Korean war was on and the armies of countries allied with South Korea were most apprehensive about the ultimate outcome of this venture.
That situation could well have become critical and might even have touched off a third world war. It was with this in mind that the government had this act written into our statutes. At least that is what was said at the time.
The whole house, at that time, was not unwilling to trust the government and did place in the hands of the Minister of Defence Production and of the cabinet powers which were generally recognized to be extraordinary and more in keeping with a dictatorship than with a democratic form of government. In fact, I do not believe that there is any country ruled by a dictator which places into the hands of one man powers more widespread than those which are to be found in chapter 62 of the Revised Statutes of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

Still, in 1951, this house did vote powers as extraordinary as those, to cope with a near desperate situation. Reading over the discussion which took place at that time, I think it may be said, to the credit of my party, that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) did point out the dangers which such legislation entailed from the point of view of our democratic freedoms and of the supremacy of parliament, and that it could only be justified by the existence of a national emergency. In that same debate, the

member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), one of the most competent Conservative members of this house, had also accepted that legislation with some misgivings and had requested that, instead of establishing a Department of Defence Production, a special branch be established under the Department of Trade and Commerce, for as he pointed out, once a new department was set up, it was very hard to do away with it later on. Here are the very words spoken by the member for Vancouver-Quadra, as reported on page 614 of Hansard for 1951:
From what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said, I take it that there is no doubt this department will be under the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and judging from press reports, and also in the light of what has happened in years gone by, that he will continue to be the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Such being the case, one might perhaps question whether this defence production could not have been carried on as a branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce rather than setting up a new department-

-because we all know that, once a department has been set up, it is very difficult to do away with it, no matter how little it may be needed. As a general rule, I think it is unwise to set up more departments of government.
Such were the views expressed by members of the Conservative party, including the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), who had also represented to the house the dangers involved in that bill.
Be that as it may, in spite of such misgivings, the bill was adopted unanimously, but on the essential condition that it be temporary. Besides, section 41 of chapter 62 clearly sets out the principle which I have just stated. It reads thus:
This act, except subsection (6) of section 4, shall expire on the 31st day of July, 1956.
Subsection 6 of section 4 deals with the retirement of the employees of the department.
The consensus of opinion was that this limitation was a sine qua non for the granting of such absolute and unlimited powers.
Today, after four years, while the act may stay in force until July 31, 1956, the house is being asked, though given no real and reasonable motives, to establish this act on a permanent basis. It is quite obvious that world tension resulting from the threat of war existing in 1951, when there was fighting in Korea, is now considerably less. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the leaders of other countries have told us repeatedly that there was good basis for optimism and that the pros-
Defence Production Act pects of peace, at this time, were quite reasonable. Last Tuesday, Sir Winston Churchill, while cautioning us against overoptimism, stated that the world situation was improving.
I think the former prime minister of the United Kingdom can be considered as an authority in this matter, and as one of those who are best able to feel the pulse of the world as to the prospects of war or peace. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said himself last week that he did not expect any war in his remaining years.

And we all know that the Prime Minister is still in the best of health. That means, Mr. Speaker, that the eventuality of war is far remote.
And at a time when the general atmosphere points to peace, the government asks us to pass an act giving it unlimited powers, even more unrestricted than those it enjoyed during the last war. It is unthinkable.

They say, or rather the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) says, that in 1951 Russia did not have the H-bomb. Could we infer, Mr. Speaker, that because Russia knows the secret of the hydrogen bomb, it might mean the end of freedom and democracy in the world? That would be an easy victory, one which had not been envisioned by the Kremlin.
Yet, that is the conclusion to which we are led by the arguments of our friends opposite. As a matter of fact, everybody recognizes that the powers granted under that act are unusual and override ordinary public law, and that such a statute is possible in a democratic country only in a national emergency, when citizens are threatened in their possessions, their persons and their freedom. That is exactly what is being said on the government side, and none of our opponents, I think, will dare contradict that statement.
On the other hand, the only explanation coming from the Minister of Defence Production and those who sit on the government benches is that liberty, individuals and property are endangered, that Russia has the hydrogen bomb.
Therefore, if one admits that this act, in its implications, overrides ordinary law, that it is dictatorial, and if it is moreover admitted that the only reason for perpetuating the legislation is the hydrogen bomb in the hands of Russia, it could be inferred that the H-bomb ends all democratic freedom. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Strange democracy!

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

The Minister of Defence Production wants to protect the freedom of the citizens of Canada against the boldness of a potential enemy and, to attain this end, the first thing he does is to abolish forever whatever freedom there is in this country.
The best reasons justifying our passing of the bill have so far been given to us by the socialist party, which has set itself up as the champion of a planned economy fully controlled by a man or an executive power, and this brought forth the plaudits of the government members who thereby showed that they had lost their faith in private enterprise.
It is not the first time that this government has acted this way, making some situations permanent which were supposed to be only temporary. It was by this same process that it achieved centralization, in general, with complete disregard for the constitution. The best example of this is that of the taxation fields which the provinces were asked to surrender temporarily at the beginning of the war and which were never returned to them.
This way of doing things is even worse in the case we are dealing with at this time, because we are asked to make permanent


powers which, as stated by the Prime Minister himself, are essentially provisional.
The government cannot blame the opposition for criticizing this act because we oppose it for the very reasons which the government gave in 1951, that is, that they cannot be permanent powers. We have been accused of filibustering. However, I must say that it was the rise of the great viziers which in turn gave birth to the filibusterers. The term has not made much headway in public opinion. The press generally, even that slightly inclined towards the government, is unanimous in stating that, at the present time, the opposition is doing its duty, that the act goes too far, and that the bill now before the house is certainly one of the most far-reaching measures that the house has had to study for a long time.
We may need a defence production department. The opposition is ready to facilitate the setting up of such a department, provided the minister in charge is given no more power than other cabinet ministers.
It is even possible that the minister really needs at present the extraordinary powers granted by the act, but since it remains in force until July 31, 1956, and since in the meantime another session will be convened, it will then be possible if necessary to extend those powers. If, at that time, the minister is able to establish in a more precise manner than he did this year the existence of a state of national emergency, the opposition will be pleased to extend those powers for a further period.
I urge the government members to forget for a moment the heat which oppresses us on these late June days and to read at leisure, without preconceived political ideas, chapter 62 of the Revised Statutes of Canada in order to establish if it really makes sense and if it is appropriate to write permanently into our legislation a measure which is the very negation of democracy.

Defence Production Act of its special authority, and then ask for a further limited extension if it thinks that is necessary. If parliament grants the indefinite extension now being sought, it may find it extremely difficult to re-establish its own theoretically overriding authority in this field.
The press across Canada, with few exceptions, views with disfavour the elimination of an expiry date from the Defence Production Act. They see that it would be treading on the very roots of our independent way of living. Perhaps it is necessary during wartime to free parliament from the need for passing upon such emergency measures as they come up. But to make it possible for the government or any department of government, through its minister, to have such powers indefinitely, as is suggested now, is very dangerous.
I am sure we all agree that the present minister is responsible, able, and quite unlikely to take advantage of these powers in peacetime. But this is beside the fact. There is no justification for the extension of the Defence Production Act indefinitely, and it is a dangerous step for any parliament to take. Parliament should be jealous of its powers as the supreme law-making body in Canada.
My deskmate, the hon. member for Dan-forth (Mr. Small), drew the attention of the house to many words and acts that have been discarded from our constitution in the last few years. These facts recall to our minds how easily our democratic way of life can slip away. Many clauses of the act have been recited by hon. members, but I should like to direct the attention of the house to section 5:
The minister may authorize any person, on his behalf or under his control and direction, to do any act or thing or to exercise any powers that the minister may do or exercise under this act.
Under section 5 the minister may employ many persons as directors or superintendents to be travelling up and down this country, spending more time on trains and in cars than they would at any given point. If the minister or his successor is so inclined, what political plums could be made out of this act.
Then, I refer to section 6 which reads:
The governor in council may appoint advisers and establish advisory and other boards, composed of such members as he may appoint, to advise or aid the minister, to perform such duties and exercise such powers as he may designate, and may fix the remuneration and expenses to be paid to persons appointed under this section.
I say in all seriousness that now would be a wonderful time for the governor in council to appoint an adviser to advise the minister and the government of the utter folly of this bill at this time.

Defence Production Act
Lastly, I refer to section 41 which reads:
This act, except subsection (6) of section 4, shall expire on the 31st day of July, 1956.
We on this side of the house fight the permanent right being given a minister to requisition supplies, and, worst of all, to appoint controllers to operate businesses. In fact, he has the control of nearly all of our economy if he so desires under this Defence Production Act.
I cannot see why the minister is so anxious that this bill be passed now, when it does not expire until July 31, 1956. There will be another full session of parliament before that time. When we renew our driver's licence, or our fire insurance, we do not do it until near the expiry date. So why the hurry now? Is the minister afraid there may be a change of mind among his party supporters in the house before that time?
I am not sure that all the members on the government side of the house are so anxious that this bill be passed now. In fact, from comments we see in the press we are led to believe that many of the hon. members of the other place are preparing to launch a determined attack on this mischievous bill, and it is quite apparent from the everlasting silence among government supporters that they are lukewarm, and I have no doubt that by now they wish that they had never heard of section 41 of the Defence Production Act, after reading all the editorials and comments of the press, regardless of political affiliations.
The content of this act is to give the minister absolute power in time of emergency, when the nation is fighting with its back to the wall, when the total mobilization of all our economic resources, and everything contained within our boundaries, is absolutely necessary to carry on a total war. But we are not at war now. Indeed, the government has all the powers at its disposal under other emergency acts to prepare in a sizeable way for any threat of an emergency. In fact, I have all kinds of confidence in our industrialists, industrial workers, and the people of this dominion, to take care of the needs of our defence production now or at any other time, except perhaps in an allout total war effort.
This bill is striking at the very foundation of our democracy which we, as a democratic people, have enjoyed since the day of Magna Carta. We, the people of Canada, like to be free to do and act as our own dictates direct us, and I believe if we are left alone we will not do too badly.
What I am afraid of is that, if too much power is given to any one department or


combination of departments, it may intimidate the industrialists and even the industrial workers, perhaps politically. And, heaven knows, we do not want that to happen.
I notice that the hon. members to my left are wholly in support of this bill-naturally, as it is right down their alley, giving the government in power sole control. I suppose they think that if they ever get in control of the reins of government this is one act that will be there waiting for them. But I use the word "if"; for if their gains are one in each four years, as it was in a recent election, they will be over four hundred years attaining that goal.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I do so somewhat with hesitation. During the days of this debate on Bill No. 256, which is an act to amend the Defence Production Act, I have listened with interest to the reasons as to why this act should not be amended at this particular time. We should all be familiar with the fact that this act does not expire until July 31, 1956. We, as elected representatives, are the spokesmen for the constituencies we represent. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is my sincere and firm conviction that the people I represent do not want these overwhelming powers, powers which, if this bill is passed, will be vested in one man, and that man is the Minister of Defence Production. Now, it may not be the present minister for very long, but it will be some minister of defence production.
It has been stated, and I am sure repeated many times in this house, that the emergency powers in this bill were given when the Korean war was in progress. The Korean war is now over, and has been for some time, and we have been told in this very house that the danger of war now is much less imminent than it was six months or even a year ago.

Last week when the member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) was speaking he used the expression "why" quite frequently during his remarks in the debate. This little question "why" is one we all like to use, especially for information purposes. I am sure we all used this word many, many times when we were children. For as long as I live I know I shall ask questions to seek to know what I do not know. How well I remember how inquisitive I was as a child. If a stranger came to our home I would soon be at his side asking questions. As I think of it now, I am sure it was a good sign, although undoubtedly it made me a nuisance many a time.
I do not know how any of us can expect to gain any knowledge without asking questions and delving into all sorts of books for new information. I am interested in outdoor life and I keep reading books on birds, animals, flowers, trees, countries and people. With a world of interest all about us, it is quite possible that we learn something new and something interesting every day of our lives.
It was the quality of curiosity which obsessed the mind of the late Thomas A. Edison and made him the great inventor he was. He wanted to find out; and it often took him thousands of tries before he arrived at the final solution. We have all noted the building of great structures, with modern means of lifting steel high into the air. Always there is a crowd on the street watching every move, wanting to know the why of it. We like to know how and why all important things are done. People who are curious are alive. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I might say that we are more than curious on this side of the house. We are desirous of knowing why the Minister of Defence Production wants these overwhelming powers, not for one year, not for three years, but forever.
The lust for power is insatiable. Give a man authority over his neighbours and at the first opportunity he will be back for more power to make effective the power he already has. Many members on the government side of the house seem to be bothered by the repetitive nature of the speeches and arguments advanced in support of freedom. I can just imagine them saying when we get up to speak "Is this another speech, or the same old arguments where the same ideas will be hashed over again"?
Life is to a large extent a repetitive process. We all derive enjoyment and stimulation from hearing old songs, attending familiar operas, rereading favourite books and looking at well beloved pictures. The virtue and the need of repetition and reiteration in stating the case 50433-3391
Defence Production Act for liberty is that liberty is not something that we can win once and for all time and, having won it, sit back to rest and enjoy it. It is like a vineyard that needs to be cultivated and constantly attended. If neglected it can become overrun by obnoxious weeds, and there is always danger from the little foxes who can spoil the vines, the vines that have tender grapes.
In reviewing the editorial comments in the daily press in Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and in summing up these editorials, it seems to be the general opinion that Canadians are slipping a little bit at a time into a state-controlled economy. It is time we as Canadians woke up and gave serious thought to these overwhelming powers to be given, not to cabinet to be passed by order in council, but to one man, the Minister of Defence Production. I believe that most of us in this house are in agreement that the Minister of Defence Production has had these controls for five years, and I am sure we all agree that he has not overexercised his authority under this act, but I am sure we are all also aware of the fact that the present minister will not be here forever and the man who succeeds him in office may be more desirous of putting into effect these powers if they are granted, which would have an effect on the life of every Canadian.
I recall during the years of the war when prices on all commodities were frozen at a level and farmers in general were asked to produce more than they had ever produced before. They went out and did this. They increased production with less help than they had been accustomed to having. Canada has gone through two world wars, in both of which the government took control of prices in order to keep them down. Scarcities were created in both wars and the government, in order to encourage increased production, had to raise the prices allowed to the farmers, but it never raised them as high as they would have gone if there had been no controls. If anyone doubts this, let him compare the price in the United States where no controls were in effect. The highest price Canadians received during that war was $2.21 per bushel and the price they received in the United States was considerably over $3.00 per bushel. Some farmers believe they are the victims of wicked men who manipulate the markets to their own advantage but to the farmers' disadvantage. Others believe they suffer more from the leadership of vain and foolish men who fancy themselves capable of running the farmers' affairs and bossing them right into paradise if given authority to do so.

Mr. Speaker, the minister will have to wait a few minutes yet. I have listened to this debate. I know a great deal has been said. A great deal has been said in reiteration, but, Mr. Speaker, the reason I want to join in this debate is that the issue before us, the very principle of this bill, goes to the very heart, to the very root, to the very being of our constitution and of our free parliamentary system. I want to say this to you, Mr. Speaker: Every man and woman elected to this house under our free parliamentary system should be speaking, should be raising their voices and should have something to say in the defence of our constitution and of our parliamentary system which we have had for long years, in fact for centuries. It was only about 300 or 400 years ago, which is a very short time actually in our history, that our forefathers stood in the mother of parliaments and fought this particular issue, the very principles that we are considering in this bill today. Therefore I say, Mr. Speaker, that every hon. member elected by the free will and the free vote of the people of this nation should be speaking to uphold and to extend the bulwarks of the free and magnificent institutions that we have enjoyed for centuries.
It is not a matter of the minister, nor is it a matter so much of this bill and other bills. This bill is similar to other bills. Every bill that comes before this house does to a certain extent give wide powers. This particular bill however gives the minister in charge the widest powers possible, the widest powers to go into every phase and every department of the economic and social life of this country.
In addition to giving these very wide powers, Mr. Speaker, there is no limitation upon the time during which the minister has these powers. It has been said by the minister and by other hon. members that it is very necessary to protect the country, it is very necessary to protect this nation because we live in a state of emergency, we live in a state of upheaval, we live in a state of uncertainty, and naturally we must be able to move quickly and with dexterity. Naturally, we must be able to pass laws to

manage the country, to bring forth its greatest manpower and obtain their great services.
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, we are not in an emergency. Any suggestion that we are in an emergency today is foolish and ludicrous. We know we are living in serious times, and we shall continue in that way, but actually serious times have almost become normal. Furthermore, we have passed through two great wars, the first world war, the second world war and the Korean war. I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, and the house that at that time we were able to rally together, we were able to bring all our forces together, and we fought those wars to a proper, a complete and a victorious conclusion. We are not in a different situation today. I will go farther than that and say that I am not so sure emergency powers of this kind should be granted even for a limited time, because we live in a day and age when transportation is speedy. Parliament can be called together quickly. We can come here from every part of this nation. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, in the last three days I have covered 3,800 miles in this country.
Considering that, it is abundantly evident that in a very short time, if an emergency arose, we could be brought together, we could consider these matters. Never once in our history, not during the first war, the second war or the Korean war did this parliament, the representatives of the people, refuse to vote anything that was required for defence or the necessities or emergency of this nation. Therefore I am not so sure that these emergency rights should be given under our constitution, under our freedom, under our rights, under the very reasons why we are sent down here. And why do the people of the country send us here? They send us down here and they pay us a salary to be here, to consider these things, to go into these matters and, if it is necessary, to give these very wide powers where they are required and where they can be properly handled and properly contained.
I want to tell you that the very great danger in this thing is that there is a new philosophy abroad in this country. As a matter of fact, there is a philosophy abroad in the world to which many countries have fallen prey. It has come about in a very subtle way and in a way that one hardly thinks about. If you look at the totalitarian states under dictatorships, how did the powers first come to those dictators? How did they come in Italy? How did they come in Germany? How did they come in Russia? How did they come in other parts of the world? They came about by the slow means of giving powers, by slowly giving extraordinary powers to
Defence Production Act one man, to a group of men or to a coterie of men. We are living in a day and age where one man or a group of men or a coterie of men want power. They want it so that they may be able to handle things, as someone said to me, in a much more streamlined and speedier way. I want to tell you that that is the very beginning, that is the very basis, that is the very essence, that is the very start of this taking over of power. It may be very subtle, it may be very hidden, but actually it is laying the foundation and preparing the way to much greater and broader powers to be given to one man or to a group and it finally ends in a dictatorship.
It is not a case of the minister in question. It is not a case so much of this bill but of the-principle of this bill. It is not only just this bill; we know that there will be something else. Larger and broader and wider powers will be asked for. As I say, it is a very dangerous philosophy that is growing in the world and is taking root subtly but surely and gradually, and very definitely it is taking root in this country and in this parliament of Canada.
I remember a very prominent person in this country, a man of ability, a man of good quality thinking, once saying to me that the day and age of parliamentary debate and parliamentary argument had come to an end, that we could not have it because we have not the time. It was argued that we have too much work to do in this country, that we have too much business to do in this country, that we must streamline our business and give it over to a few experts. It is argued that there is no need for this discussion and this debate on this bill.
I want to say to you and to all members of this house that after all this is not what we have lived and fought for, this is not what our ancestors fought for for hundreds of years.. We are advocating the retaining of those very principles. Call it a filibuster if you like;: I am glad to be in a filibuster if its purpose-is to guard those principles of democracy and! our democratic institutions. Those are what we want to uphold in the years to come.
When I look across at the minister I cannot help remembering that on a great many occasions he has been more than good to me. I regard him most highly; I have the highest respect for him. But my sense of constitutional right, my sense of parliamentary right, my sense of parliamentary freedom must always override any personal feelings that I may have.
I think the minister himself, and surely hon. members sitting opposite when looking: over this bill, must realize that in giving themselves these very wide powers they are-
5370	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act taking on a tremendous responsibility, so great that I would hardly think any one minister or any one group would want to take it on. These powers are very wide. As a matter of fact, if this bill passes and these powers are granted for an indefinite period certain phases of our parliamentary government will have passed away, will be gone entirely.
The minister could go out and take over any business in this country that he wished to take over. He could take over the railroads, he could take over the hydroelectric power facilities, he could take over any private industry. He could take over the press, and I should think they would be greatly alarmed about that because after all they have been the great proponents of freedom in this nation. We welcome that, and that is what it should always be. But these things can be done. In addition to that he can order any person that he should choose, not he himself with his particular and peculiar ability but anyone he chooses to go into any industry to manage that industry. But the dreadful part of it all is that that person will not be responsible to the former owner and would not be responsible actually to anyone. Certainly he would not be responsible to the people or to their elected representatives.
To my mind that sets a very bad example. It sets a very bad example to Canadian business and to Canadian institutions in the method of carrying on our institutions. I suppose it will be said that recourse could be taken to the courts in an action against the crown, but every hon. member here, particularly those who adhere to the law profession, know how foolish and how impossible it is to take action against the crown. You do not get very far in any action against the crown.
Then I say with the greatest deference that the minister and the whole government would be laid open to pressure from different groups. After all we are only human beings and this pressure possibility is one of the dangerous aspects of this bill. Somebody might want more steel or something else and he would come to the controller or the person in control to get his steel. Then of course he would feel that he must make a large return at certain times. Human nature being what it is, that is the sort of thing which makes our parliamentary practices corrupt and improper. We are here in this democratic country today with our democratic institutions and we should be able to show the world that we are able to .carry on, that we are able to move through


free enterprise, through the freedom of man, to think and to do and to give of our very best.
I want to take issue at this moment with those to the left of me. It is improper and unfair to make any suggestions that in the Korean war or in the first and second great wars any part of this country was sabotaged by any groups or persons. That is not true. We know that leaders of industry and men working in industry, from the very top to the very bottom, gave the very best of everything they had to the winning of this war and supported the men and women who went out and fought on the fronts for us, who fought for that particular freedom for which I am speaking in this house today.
I should like to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to every hon. member of this house, and to the people of Canada, that I do not intend to go home to my constituency and tell the people, some 55,000 people, that I for one moment allowed myself to give in in any way, to procrastinate, or to have any doubts as to where I stand, because I stand for the free parliamentary institutions of this nation. They have been with us for hundreds of years and it is my pride that I can play some part in maintaining them. I intend to vote for them to be with us for many more sessions. For that reason I cannot and will not be found supporting a bill of this kind.

The circumstances under which this bill was brought before this house and the ideas behind it certainly are entitled to very grave consideration by the members of this parliament and by the country in general. I remember when the defence production bill was before the house in 1951 and I also remember that our party voted for it and I personally voted for it. I did so for two reasons. The first was that I felt that such an act was necessary under conditions such as were prevailing at that time. But I had another reason as well, and that reason was mentioned at the time. That was that I had hoped, along with many other members

from my part of the country, that under the vast powers which were then given to the Minister of Defence Production there would be some decentralization of industry across this country.
We felt that it would be a good thing for Canada, and we also felt that the production could have been just as effectively carried out if all parts of Canada were given the chance to contribute. I have read the reports of the department carefully for the last five or six years, and I must say I am disappointed that there has not been more decentralization of industry. I am greatly disappointed that my section of the country in particular has not been able to make the contribution it could make and would like to make to this department. It has been the same old story. Every two weeks we get a report from the Department of Defence Production that millions of dollars are spent for products of defence in and around Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton and other great centres in the two large provinces. A few hundred dollars goes to other parts of Canada. I do not think it is good for Canada, and I do not think that is the way to build up a great country. As I said before, in view of the unlimited powers which were given to the minister at that time, we had every reason to hope that a different situation would have arisen.
The other day I was quite pleased, though not surprised, to see the remarks of the premier of Newfoundland in connection with this situation. I might say that the premier of Newfoundland has been in Canadian politics long enough now to have his eyes opened. He realizes that the four Atlantic provinces have a strong case for more assistance than they are getting. I think he realizes also, as I am sure the people of his province are realizing, that there is something more to this confederation, which they came into a few years ago, than the receiving of children's allowances and old age pensions. I am glad that Premier Smallwood is now championing the cause which has been so well championed by opposition members of this house over quite a period of years.

I was quite surprised, as have been many members on this side of the house-as they have all expressed in their speeches-that this bill was brought up this year. This is now the month of June. The Defence Production Act runs until the 31st of July, 1956, which is over 13 months from now. Why it was necessary at this session
Defence Production Act to push through an act of this kind is beyond the comprehension of a good many members in this house.
I was also quite surprised, after it was brought before this house and after it was seen that there was very strong sentiment from one end of this country to the other against this bill, that it has not been withdrawn either by the Prime Minister or by the Minister of Defence Production. I join with others in expressing my surprise that the Prime Minister of this country, who was responsible for introducing this bill in the house, has not as yet seen fit to rise in the house and give us some of his ideas upon a bill of this kind, which is his own bill. As the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) mentioned a few days ago, the Prime Minister of this country is one of the leading jurists of Canada and has been for a great many years a man whose ideas are highly respected, and a great constitutional lawyer. I am sure that in his heart of hearts he realizes, as many others do across Canada, that this bill does or will affect the freedoms of a great many people.
As was indicated this morning when one of our members rose to speak, the government members are a little annoyed by the continuing of this debate. I wish to say that the fault is theirs. The fault is not of the opposition members. This debate could have ended long ago. All they needed to do was to get up and say that they agreed that the setting up of this defence production department is necessary but these unheard of powers, except in wartime, for which the minister is asking, should not be continued permanently in Canada. If that had been done this debate would have ended many days ago. The people are not quiet despite the fact that government members may think so. It takes a long time in this country for the people to realize what is happening. In spite of all this reaction from one end of Canada to the other, what does the minister tell us? We heard him the other day. His excuse for asking for these powers is that the Russians have the hydrogen bomb. Certainly they have the hydrogen bomb. We have the hydrogen bomb.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.
I am speaking now of the nations allied with us, the NATO nations. The United States and Great Britain have the hydrogen bomb.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Keep to the United States.

I do not have to keep to the United States. We are all one. I am speaking of the free peoples of the world. We, the free people, have the hydrogen bomb, and surely we would act together in case of war. In fact, Canada probably could have had the hydrogen bomb but it was too expensive and we knew we could get hydrogen bombs from the United States if we needed them for defence. My understanding is that Great Britain has the hydrogen bomb. The minister shakes his head. I will take his word for it, but in any event there is no doubt in my mind, nor do I think there is any doubt in the minds of the people of this country or of the free world that we, the free people of the world, have more hydrogen bombs than the Russians. As one speaker said, if it ever comes to the stage that hydrogen bombs are dropped on Canada or some place else then it will not make any difference whether or not we have these emergency powers. I should like to read a short article from Time magazine of June 27 setting forth what Mr. Dulles says.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Order.
You had better wait until you hear what is in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You had better not read it.
It does not have to do with the defence production bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the rule has been enforced many times that opinions of people outside this house bearing on the business of the house are out of order.
That is not what it is.

The minister does not know any more about what I am going to read than he does about some other matters. As a matter of fact it has no bearing on the house debates. It is what Mr. Dulles said a few days ago. The article reads:
Russia, Dulles said, was faced with bankruptcy of its old policy. Cold war and hot threats had failed to cow western Europe or to halt the rebirth of a rearmed, democratic Germany. The Soviets were over-committed . . .
The article goes on to point out that Russia has less than a third of United States industrial capacity. It is for that reason I say there is no doubt in my mind that the United States has far more hydrogen bombs than Russia. There are just two things the Russians understand and only one for which they have any great respect. There is no question that they have respect for strength. We all know that the attitude of the Russian people today seems to be changing. The opinion is that the reason it is changing is that they realize the western world is becoming stronger day by day.
We believe in the Defence Production Act so far as the setting up of a department is concerned. That has been said in the house a good many times. There is no objection to that. We certainly believe the situation is serious enough for such an act.
Now, I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that never before in any act of this nature has there not been a time limit. In his day the Minister of Defence Production has had more power, I imagine, than any other man who has ever lived in Canada. But in the acts that were placed upon the statute books in 1939, at the beginning of the war, such as the munitions and supply act which gave the minister great powers, and they were needed, we find such sections as section 16 of that act. It reads:
Subject to the following provisions of this section, the foregoing provisions of this act shall continue in force for a period of three years beginning with the date of the passing of this act, and shall then expire:
That is the munitions and supply act in 1939 and 1940, and it was allowed to remain on the statute books for three years.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What happened in 1943?

I will tell you what happened.
Defence Production Act

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That clause was taken out.

In 1943, the munitions and supply act contained section 17 which read as follows:
Subject to the following provisions of this section, the foregoing provisions of this act shall continue in force for a period of three years beginning with the date of the passing of this act, and shall then expire;
That was in the munitions and supply act in 1939 and 1940, an act which was passed during a very serious time in this country and when we were in the midst of one of the greatest wars in history.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I should like to call the attention of the house to an act which set up the department of reconstruction. You will all remember that this was in 1944-45 and the act contained practically unlimited powers which were given to the minister at that time. There was a great scarcity of goods in this country and it was necessary for the minister, in dealing with reconstruction, to have these powers.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think my hon. friend was quoting the 1943 amendment. My understanding is the amendment at that time was retroactive to April 9, 1940 and the section relating to expiry was repealed, to be effective as of April 9, 1940.
For another three years.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, the expiry date was repealed in 1943.
At any rate, the act is now off the books.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes, and it was
taken off in 1950 by action of the Liberal government, without any suggestion from the Conservative party.
Why don't you do that now?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We will, when we get through with it.
That is what you want, power to put it in and take it out.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
Without worrying about parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The trouble is you think you are parliament.

We know you are not; you are anti-parliament, that is the trouble.

Defence Production Act

In the statutes of 1940, chapter 31, section 10, we find the following in the department of munitions and supply act:
Subsection 1 of section 16 of the said act (renumbered as section 17 by subsection 2 of this section) is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"17. (1) Subject to the following provisions of this section, the foregoing provisions of this act shall continue in force for a period of three years beginning with the date of the passing of this act, and shall then expire;
It seems to me that is definite enough, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: For a lawyer, you have not read that act very thoroughly.

Well, I have read the section very carefully. As I say, Mr. Speaker, the department of reconstruction act, chapter 18 of the statutes of 1944-45, section 14, says:
This act shall continue in force during the period of reconstruction.
As the minister knows, the date of expiry for reconstruction was 1949. In effect, therefore, that section says this act shall continue until 1949.
The essential materials act, another very important act and one which gave the minister very broad powers, contains section 10, which reads:
This act shall expire on the thirty-first day of July. 1952.
This act was chapter 6 of the statutes of 1950-51. All these acts had a definite expiry date, Mr. Speaker, as I am contending this act should have. The minister has been given tremendous powers. The minister and some of those who are sitting on the other side try to make us believe that the emergency is as great today as it was in 1951. It would take considerable time to go over the situation as it was in 1951 and previous to that time. To understand the situation in 1951, one should review the happenings of the previous years.
We recall that in 1946, for instance, Sir Winston Churchill was very much concerned about the lack of interest of the people throughout the world in the growth of communism. We all remember that he made a speech at Fulton, Missouri, and he alerted the people to what the possibilities were so far as communism in this country was concerned. He told them how Russia had taken over Poland, Czechoslovakia, the Balkan states, East Germany, and how in all these countries large armies were being built up by the Russians. Russia herself maintained a very large army, a navy and an air force. The United States, Great Britain and the other free nations, up until 1951, were more or less indifferent. We all know that at that 

time West Germany, one of the great nations before the great war and which is probably becoming a great nation today, was prostrate. Austria was occupied. Italy and Yugoslavia were unfriendly as a result of the difficulty over Trieste. This was the situation from 1946 to 1951, and it continued after that.
The only salvation we had at that time, as expressed by Sir Winston Churchill, was the atomic bomb; that was the salvation of this world in 1951. Then, there was the Korean war. I do not think there is any member in this house or anyone in Canada who understands a situation who will not say that was an extremely serious time and that there was a great emergency in Canada. The war had been started. At that time Canada, the United States and Great Britain did not know whether or not Russia would go to war over the Korean situation. We had no idea. Indeed, there was a great emergency in 1951, when this act was passed.
What is the situation today, in 1955? The Korean war is ended. The difficulties in Trieste are settled. Italy and Yugoslavia are friendly and, so far as we know, they are friendly towards the great western powers. Austria is a neutral country. The situation in Malaya today is better than it has been for a good many months. The whole picture in the world today is much better than it was in 1951. Besides that, look at the allies that the western nations have today. Western Germany, for instance, which in 1951 was almost prostrate before Russia, is today a great nation and capable of producing large armies, and seems to be willing to do so. There is a better feeling in Turkey, Spain, Pakistan and all these nations. And I want to say to the minister that I do not believe he or any of his supporters can convince anyone in this House of Commons or in the country that there is today the emergency that there was in 1951.
In that connection I should like to quote what Chancellor Adenauer said the other day with respect to the world situation. Speaking of today he said:
The climate is more favourable for the reason that the West, the free peoples, are now stronger than they were previously. They have grown stronger through the unity which has been achieved in Europe by the conclusion of the Western European Union and by the entry of the Federal Republic into the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
Then the article goes on to say:
He contrasted the growing strength and unity of the free world with the demands posed upon the Soviet Union "by its internal economic tasks". To mend its internal difficulties, he said, the Soviet Union needs "a lengthy pause for relaxation".
Continuing his note of optimism, he spoke of an "unmistakable repudiation of communism by the

greater part of Asia; thus the Soviet Union can no longer reckon that the majority of the peoples of Asia stand behind her".
Does that sound as though there was a greater emergency, or one anywhere near comparable, either in Canada or in the western world, with that of 1951?
Now, attention has been drawn a number of times to those who are defending this bill in the house. The great defence that has come to the minister and the government in defence of this bill has not been from the Liberal party. It has not come from members on the government side of the house; it is from the socialist party in this House of Commons. And that is just as we would expect, because it is right down their alley. This is more or less a socialistic measure in peacetime.
The C.C.F. have always been in favour of controls. That is part of the philosophy of the C.C.F. party-the control of business. They believe in the control of business. As a matter of fact they believe in the extermination of free enterprise in this country. They believe in government taking over control.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You want business to control the country.
No; but so long as business is honest, as I believe it is in Canada, they have a great part to play in the controlling of the country. There is no question about that.
What about combines investigations?

As proof of what 1 say, what did the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) do? He quoted one instance, the instance of some clothing company at the time of the first war. He said the minister had said that one company had refused to produce clothing, and he proceeded to base his argument upon that one case.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Surely the hon. member
realizes that the quotation I gave from the minister was not with respect to just one company. He said no contracts had been let under the profits limitation clause.

If the hon. member will look at it he will find that it was the only definite case the hon. member quoted. He did mention something about fabricated steel. Then he quoted the minister, in a later statement, as saying that the companies controlling the fabricated steel industry in this country could be depended upon.
And the same line was followed by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough). His main argument was to
Defence Production Act insult industry in this country and to try to insult the Conservative party. But we are pretty thick-skinned and we did not mind what he said.
Then along came the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott). Well, he did not put up any argument in this house which would defend the attitude of the government.
I might add this, that I believe the hon. member for Vancouver South was at one time a socialist; and when he was a socialist he was very strong in the defence of socialist principles. But now he can always find something good in everything this government does. In fact, he is the greatest defender of the Liberal faith in the House of Commons. He can always stand up and find some argument in defence of what the government does. I believe if the minister were to bring in a bill to scuttle the whole House of Commons the hon. member for Vancouver South would stand up and find some good and substantial reason as to why it should be done.
Then the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) is the minister's parliamentary assistant and, of course, he has a duty to perform. His duty, of course, is to try to protect the minister in every way he can. He defended the bill.
Mr. Speaker, the argument as to why this act should be continued has been, mostly, that the Russians have the hydrogen bomb, and that industry in this country is so dishonest that it cannot be trusted. I have been very much surprised, in view of the fact that there are some outstanding businessmen among the members supporting the government-many outstanding Liberal businessmen-that some member of the Liberal party has not seen fit to get up and defend industry in this country.
They call themselves the free enterprise party. Well, if such is the case, why do they not defend free enterprise?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Your leader called them merchants of death.

If this bill passes in its present form it will be the best propaganda that the socialist party has ever had in this Dominion of Canada-and it is being supported by the Liberal party which, as I said a moment ago, calls itself the free enterprise party.
