Mr. Speaker, I find I have only a few more minutes left. There are many more things I should like to say. At one o'clock I was speaking about the arguments made by the government about the continuing of these powers. There was one further argument used particularly by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) and the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith). It had to do with electronics. I have no time to enlarge on their arguments nor to quote what they said, but I should like to refer hon. members to the report of the Department of Defence Production for 1954. On page 21, which deals with the electronics branch, they will find that the report made by the department was to the effect that everything was in excellent shape as far as production and requirements of electronics were concerned. I intended to read this to the house but I have not time this afternoon.
I contend that no concrete case has been made for the continuance of those powers. There is just the bare assertion by the minister that we want them and we are going to have them. I do not think that is good enough for this parliament of Canada, nor do I think it is good enough for the people of Canada. Taking that into consideration, Mr. Speaker, I wish to move the following amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard):
That Bill No. 256, an act to amend the Defence Production Act, be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce with instructions that they have power to examine and report upon the advisability of
(a)	placing the Department of Defence Production on a permanent basis and conferring on the department such powers as ought to be of a continuing nature; and
(b)	conferring for a period of one year, or until extended by parliament, such additional powers as may be strictly necessary in the light of the existing world conditions.
I contend that the continuance of those powers permanently or for an indefinite period is a positive threat, a threat held over the heads of industry and labour in this country. I also contend, Mr. Speaker, that it is not necessary to threaten the Canadian people. I contend it is not good psychology to do so. The people of Canada have always done things voluntarily and I believe that if this is left on a voluntary basis the people of Canada will again respond as they have done in the past. They can be trusted. There is no great emergency.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in listening to the debate I feel that I am living in another

world, or at least that the opposition in this house is debating in another world. There is nothing very new about the Defence Production Act. It has been in force now for 16 years in this country, with the exception of a little less than a year after the munitions and supply act was repealed by this government, and I may say repealed by this government with no prompting from the Conservative party. It was repealed because it was felt that that particular act was no longer needed.
Hon. members may say that the Defence Production Act is not the munitions and supply act. However, there is nothing in the Defence Production Act that was not in the munitions and supply act, although the powers granted the department in the munitions and supply act were much more extensive than those in the act now under discussion.
This debate arises out of a very simple amendment to the Defence Production Act. The amendment provides that the Department of Defence Production shall be permanent. Everyone seems to agree that the Department of Defence Production should be permanent. While hon. members tell us that the crisis is over, there is no more threat to the security of Canada, nevertheless the business of the Department of Defence Production has shown no falling off whatever.
If the Department of Defence Production is to be made permanent, it seems logical to me that the act upon which the department depends for its authority should also be made permanent.
The departmental act, and the act of any department, sets out the duties and obligations of the department and the authority under which the department carries out those duties and obligations. To say that the Department of Defence Production can be made permanent without a permanent Defence Production Act is to say that the Department of Public Works can be a permanent department even though the Public Works Act is temporary in nature, or that the Department of National Revenue can be a permanent department if the Department of National Revenue Act is a temporary act, or that the post office can be a permanent department if the Post Office Act is a temporary act. That is the simple purpose of the bill. It is following logic. This introduces no to the Defence Production Act introduces no new controls over industry, and incidentally it introduces no controls whatever over persons.
Industry is familiar with these controls. It has been working under them for 16 years,
Defence Production Act
and as far as I know it is quite happy to work under them indefinitely. Of all the complaints that have been heard since this debate started I have heard not one single complaint from the people affected, namely, the people who are actually doing the defence production work in this country.
What has happened? We have seen any legitimate objections to the bill drowned in a torrent of exaggeration, and the corpses of the arguments are now floating around in a vast ocean of words.
If at this stage anyone knows what the argument against the bill is I am sure that I cannot be one of that number.
Nobody knows the arguments for it.
Take a look at the Winnipeg Free Press.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am about to come to the arguments. I have culled a few gems from this debate. I spoke about exaggeration. Here are a few examples: "There has not been a greater issue before the House of Commons since this house was set up under the British North America Act in 1867." Then hon. members opposite went back and compared this amendment with the King Henry VIII clause, the clause which gave the king absolute power. "It is a reversion to something that has not happened since the days of the Tudors and the Stuarts." This is another gem: "It will lead our people into slavery." "It has not been necessary once in the last two years, yet hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent on defence requirements." That is the nature of the exaggerations.
What is the history of this act? It was first introduced, not by myself or by anyone in the department over which I was then minister, but was brought before parliament by my former colleague, the Hon. J. L. Ralston, who was then minister of finance, and was assented to on September 13, 1939. The act contained an expiry date of three years from date of enactment.
In 1943 an amendment was brought in which cancelled the expiry date, just what we are asking to have done at this time. That amendment passed the house with practically no debate and from that day on the munitions and supply act was a permanent act of the government of Canada. The department of munitions and supply was dismantled in 1947 and 1948 and the act became inoperative. In 1950 the munitions and supply act was repealed and was replaced by the Defence Supplies Act. In 1951 the Defence Supplies Act was suspended and in that year the
5378	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act Defence Production Act was passed with an expiry date of 1956. That is the simple history of this legislation.
What is the purpose of the Defence Production Act? The act does two things. First it gives the government control over critical supplies required for the defence program. It has been said that the supplies and services act of the United Kingdom is less drastic than the act we are now discussing. I think anyone who is familiar with both acts will say that the powers in the supplies and services act are more drastic than anything contained in the act now under discussion. The defence production act of the United States is much more comprehensive and grants powers which we feel are not required in this country.
People say that we do not need the provision giving control over strategic raw materials. I can tell hon. members that nickel, which is vital to defence, is one metal which is in short supply throughout the world. There is no formal control over nickel in this country and in that regard we are unique because every country except Canada has control over the supply of nickel.
The reason we have not applied control to this metal here is that the users are familiar with our power to apply control and therefore have been careful to live up to the international rules for the use of nickel. There is a great temptation to step out of line. Nickel is being sold in this country for 64 cents a pound and the European price is $1.50 per pound. Any quantity of nickel can be contracted for in Europe for that price. It is a great temptation for someone in this country to obtain nickel, not to be used in his own production but to be exported to Europe. Such is the regard for the law among our metals and munitions people that we have had no indication that that has taken place. The consumption of nickel has risen very sharply in this country but we have kept careful check on its use and have found nothing to indicate that the uses of the metal are not entirely legitimate. That is one strategic metal in short supply.
Copper is another metal in short supply and prices of copper in Europe are considerably higher than they are in Canada. Other metals are tottering on the verge of being in short supply. We conceive it to be the duty of the Department of Defence Production to see that there is sufficient for defence requirements and that the balance is allocated fairly among all users of the metal. That is the purpose of that part of the Defence Production Act which gives the right to ration scarce materials.
That right is not being used formally at the moment, but it is being used informally. We
[Mr. Howe (Port Arthur).!

required steel for the mid-Canada line. We said to the steel companies that we must have our steel requirements in the interests of national defence and that they would have to set aside or postpone civilian orders in order to give us this steel when we needed it for this most essential defence project. That has been done and there has been no need for formal government action. As I say, that procedure is one way of handling a well-disciplined munitions industry.
Other provisions of the act affect property, but there is no provision in the Defence Production Act that affects the freedom of any person. It gives the government the right, if required for the defence of Canada, to take over the production facilities of certain defence manufacturers. That is the sole effect of the balance of the act. When people rant about the freedom of the individual, I defy anyone to show me one section in the act which affects the freedom of the individual. It does affect the property of the individual, but under the act no property can be taken without compensation. Everywhere in the act it is made quite clear that if property is taken, it must be taken for the purposes of national defence and for no other purpose. Proper compensation will be allocated, either by the government directly or through the courts of the land.
An hon. member asks why it is necessary to have these powers, since we have a good munitions industry in this country. I say "Amen" to that. No country in the world has a stronger and more devoted munitions industry than Canada. In that connection I dissociate myself entirely from the criticism of the industry made by members of the C.C.F. party.
Canada's defence industry and I have worked together for the 16 years I have been responsible for the procurement of defence supplies. I have been in difficulties during that time but I have never had the slightest trouble in getting industry as a whole to come to my help in a united effort to work out a solution. Standing here today I am very proud of the fact that in those 16 years I have never undertaken to produce any munitions of war which I have not been able to produce and produce within a reasonable period of time.
The minister does not agree with the Minister of Fisheries?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I did not interrupt the hon. member very much.
You interrupted everybody else.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
What are the problems for which this act is required? A great deal has been said about clothing, with particular reference to nylon stockings and underwear. I suppose that those references are the result of the heat, as I cannot think of any other reason why that would be the subject of conversation here. However, they have been referred to several times as important purchasing problems.
Last year the department purchased, either for Canadian defence purposes or for foreign governments, about $1,025 million worth of material. Twenty million dollars of that was spent for the purchase of clothing; about $100 million was for what we call shelf articles, that is, food and supplies which are readily purchasable through ordinary channels. We do not need this act at all for that kind of purchasing. If that were the extent of the duties of the department, we would not need this act. As a matter of fact, when such purchasing was mainly the responsibility of the department in 1947 and 1948 we disbanded the department of munitions and supply.
However, the other $900 million of expenditure last year was for weapons, and largely for weapons that were new and had to be developed by industry. Development work is very difficult work to supervise. The army develops an idea of what it wants and reduces that idea to an outline plan and specification. Then it is given to an industry to develop, and the cost of development is paid for by the government.
Fantastically large sums are sometimes put out for that development work. It has been said here by several opposition members, "Why worry about the money? We give you all the money you ask for". I do not know whether they were thinking about the amounts of money I am talking about, but I can just tell you this. In the case of the Orenda engine and the CF-100 aircraft we had paid A. V. Roe company $122 million before the first finished aircraft was delivered. Perhaps some of you have had the experience of being responsible for $30 or $40 million of other people's money in a development enterprise that is going bad and looks as though it would fail. If that development project fails at that point, the returns to the government are exactly zero. It is a development contract and if the development cannot be carried out, the money is gone.
The Leader of the Opposition said that the expression "All or nothing" is a quotation from the musical comedy "Oklahoma". I did not know that. I will admit he is the expert on musical comedies. That is the situation
Defence Production Act with development work "all or nothing". Either you get a successful development or the money is gone. I can tell you that in carrying out that same A. V. Roe development contract there were anxious moments. After we had got involved for $30 or $40 million it was quite obvious that the management of that day was not likely to produce what we required. The top management of A. V. Roe was resident in England. The men on the job just did not have the experience necessary to carry out the work, and that became obvious to all concerned.
Consequently we took steps to strengthen the management. We called the president and managing director of the company to Canada and said, "Look here, this is not good enough. Your local management must be strengthened". He asked "where can we obtain qualified men?" We started off by suggesting the co-ordinator of defence production from our own department, and he today is president of the company and a very efficient president. We intervened with General Motors and persuaded them to lend us their No. 2 man from the Allison engine works. He came to Canada and worked for two years on the development work. Other qualified men were obtained from industry. I may say that industry co-operated to the full, and, as I said before, I have never known Canadian industry to see the Department of Defence Production in a jam without being willing to do whatever was needed to make their contribution to solving the dilemma.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The present top man of the Orenda engine works is a man we supplied from the Department of Defence Production to take over that work. He was our director of electronics in the department. But the purpose of the act is to make sure that when we find a situation of that kind, where great sums of the taxpayers' money is at stake, we can direct the strength of the Canadian industry into the problem, and save the government's expenditure and produce the munitions which the department of defence is requiring at that time. That is the story of $122 million of public money invested in development work with the Avro company, and the Avro company today is in my opinion the equal in management strength, design strength and production strength of any aircraft facility on this continent.
We had another situation. We had a requirement for perhaps the most complicated gun that has been produced to date in this war. This is a naval anti-aircraft gun. We had a comparatively small requirement and it

Defence Production Act was doubtful whether we could produce it economically in Canada. However, our requirement was added to by the United States government, so that we had a very sizeable order for that type of gun. It seemed to be one that warranted development and production in this country. We undertook that work and we invested about $20 million in that project before the first gun was produced. We had great production difficulties; we were confronted with reject after reject. We asked industry to help. One of the largest firms gave us the time of their president, a man I consider the top production man in this country today. He worked on the job for some time. We borrowed a metallurgist from another company. We borrowed a superintendent of production from a third company. The result was that we prevented cancellation of its order by the United States government, which would have led to a very heavy loss to the Canadian taxpayer. We finished the order, and all the money invested for development by the government of Canada was recovered. Without the Defence Production Act behind me I certainly would not have been able to deal with a situation of that kind.
You may be greatly relieved that those particular situations are behind me. I can say that now we have started on a program of development that gives me the shudders, a supersonic plane and a supersonic engine. I believe those weapons are certainly required as soon as they can be produced, to ward off the threat which hon. members opposite insist does not exist. They say, "Yes, but the atomic bomb threat is not very serious-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Nonsense! Nobody said that in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
However, we embarked on that program and already on that program we have invested $30 million. Before we get through, it will be around $100 million. That is a program no other country has carried through successfully as yet. At this time several countries are working at the same problem. As I have said, we have never missed yet. I think we are the
[Mr. Howe (Port Arthur).)

only country that can say that we have developed a fighter aircraft and have developed a powerful jet engine without a miss. I hope we do not miss this time. We will not miss if the strength of our industry, of all Canadian industry, is sufficient to achieve the objective. But I shudder to think of the problems of developments.
Some of you do not know how it feels to be out on a limb for $30 million or more of other people's money and have a serious doubt cast on the ultimate success of the program. I can tell you that you do not sleep very well until you get the situation straightened out.
You have been out on the limb for $5,000 million in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I have?
The government has been out on the limb for $5,000 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Just elucidate that. That sounds like a very wise remark and the figure sounds pretty big.
With other people's money, the taxpayers' money.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
As I say, we have these problems facing us. I have mentioned one, the new supersonic plane. We are just moving into the field of guided missiles, a field in which no country has achieved very much at the moment. That program is going to require large sums of taxpayers' money for purposes of development. That has got to be faced. As I say, if we get all Canadian industry behind each project I have confidence we can handle that problem. Certainly if a manufacturer such as Avro could have said to us-and I may say they did say it to us

"Never mind, we are satisfied with our management and if you are not that is just too bad", we could say to them, "Sorry; either you operate the plant in the way we believe will produce results or there are other ways of having it operated, for we have too much at stake here to let you decide that you do not need any help."
As I have said, the act does not affect persons. It only affects property, and only such property as is required for defence purposes. It is a good defence against the provisions of the act to say that the action taken was not necessary in the defence of Canada. As I have said, the act covers defence contracts. Therefore all the agitation we have had here is designed solely for the purpose of protecting defence contractors. They are very fine people. They are very able and co-operative, but I cannot think of any class of manufacturers in this country better able to take care of themselves than

those same defence production manufacturers. They know their production work. They know how to handle their business affairs. It is a pleasure to deal with them because they do not say: "We want you to protect us". They stand up and say: "We are able to look after ourselves".
Why are we meeting with all these efforts to protect defence contractors? It was not always so. It was not long ago that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) was writing magazine articles on the subject of defence contractors and those articles were headed, "Merchants of Death". Among the "merchants of death" who were dealt with in great style was the parent company of our own Canadair, which was then known as the Electric Boat Company. Certainly the Leader of the Opposition has suddenly adopted a warm protective attitude towards these same people whom he labelled merchants of death not so many years ago. As I say, the bill now being considered has a real use and is needed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, at no time in any article that I wrote under the heading "Merchants of Death", which was an article 1 stand by today, was there a single reference to a Canadian company. The minister knows that perfectly well and should not place that impression on the record in the way he has this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I did not say that. I said there was a reference to the parent company of Canadair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is so inaccurate that I must deal with it. It was not the parent company of Canadair at the time the article was written, and the minister well knows that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The article was written before Canadair was Canadair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In fact, it had not even been started.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You have succeeded in throwing me off the trend of my discourse.
We will give you time to get back as long as you get back straight.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It is said that the act is not needed because it has not been used for the last two years. It has been used to a limited extent. I think we have had nine prosecutions under the act and we won them all. I think other clauses have been invoked once or twice but otherwise we have not found it necessary to invoke the act. Why? Because industry has been
Defence Production Act working under the legislation for 16 years, knows the rules as well as we do and, being law-abiding people, they follow the rules. We have traffic rules in this country. They have never been invoked against me. I have been lucky, but possibly the reason they have not been invoked against me is that I think I know the rules and try to follow them. That is the reason this act has not been invoked against the manufacturers of munitions.
However, I am pointing out that in extending the life of the department it is necessary to extend the life of the rules which govern the operation of the department. That is all we are trying to do in this particular case. We have been told a good deal about the purity of the Conservative party in matters of this kind.
You are into politics now.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I think perhaps it would be worth while to take a moment or two to debunk that theory. Back in
1947	we did away with the department of munitions and supply which made the act non-operative. That act had been used by the Ontario Hydro-Electric Power Commission as protection. At their request we appointed the chairman of the commission as deputy power controller and extended the protection of the act to Ontario hydro. When the department of munitions and supply was dismantled what was done in Ontario? The power act was amended in 1947 to provide that no action could be taken against the Ontario hydro in time of emergency. Another paragraph provided that there was an emergency any time the hydro commission ruled there was an emergency. In other words, the legislation denied suppliers the right to take action in the courts against Ontario hydro in times of emergency and leaves it to hydro to say what are times of emergency. Talk about delegating the powers of government! Here there is first a denial of the courts and then a delegation of the power to declare an emergency.
However, that was not strong enough. In
1948	the matter was straightened out properly. The Leader of the Opposition, who was then premier of Ontario, brought in legislation which for all time denied access to the courts of the land to anyone dealing with Ontario hydro. Today you have a situation on the St. Lawrence river where there are two sets of contractors working. One is working for the St. Lawrence seaway authority. If there is a dispute between the authority and a contractor an appeal can be had to the courts. The courts will decide the equity of the situation and compensation will be paid accordingly. Another

Defence Production Act set of contractors is working for Ontario hydro. If there is a dispute between these contractors and the Ontario hydro they will find they are working by the law of hydro and that the decision of hydro is final and binding.
That is the rule of law.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is the rule of law as applied by a Conservative government. That is the rule of law introduced by the Leader of the Opposition who sobbed so loudly for three hours and 40 minutes at one session about this amendment.
This will be under the law of Howe.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The situation has reached the point where the government must insist that this legislation be passed. If it had been suggested earlier that it would relieve people's minds-and I think it would have relieved the minds of the Social Credi-ters-to put a time limit of five years on the legislation, that might have been considered. But we would have done it with full knowledge that another extension would be necessary, because the very development work on the supersonic planes I am talking about is a six-year program, and I am satisfied the guided missile program will go far beyond that period.
In the past we have set a time which we believed was a reasonable time limit within which the program in hand could be completed. I do not know what that time limit would be today. I know it is not five years from now. Anyway, the time for suggestions of that kind is past, and I think that hon. members can rely on the government with confidence to dispense with the act and dispense with the department as soon as either is not needed. It has been done before, and it will be done again.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in order to keep this clear in our minds, may I ask the minister a question? Will he give us the date of the order in regard to these supersonic craft which will be affected in any way by this act being suspended?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The date of the order?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister is explaining he must have this act, perhaps for five years, for this order.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The order has been placed. We did not need the act to place the order.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is no order?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There is an order, certainly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What date was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Oh, two or three months ago. Nevertheless, that development work is going on for five or six years, and the act may be required to be invoked at any time within that period to carry out that work and similar contracts for guided missiles. I have not mentioned the mid-Canada early warning line. This work is being carried out under most difficult circumstances. If supplies were required there that were not readily available, the act will be in force to obtain those supplies. Not to do so would, of course, be fatal to the completion of this urgently required project on time.
As I say, this debate is being carried on in the house and it is being carried on outside the house. After listening to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) for three hours and 40 minutes, I went home to have a quiet dinner and I listened to him on the radio.
Congratulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
His radio speech was a most passionate appeal to the public to come to his support on this bill. It reminded me of Joan of Arc supplicating the peasants of France to come to the support of her banners. I may say the exaggeration we have heard in this house was as nothing compared to the exaggeration further expanded over the radio program. I may say that it did bear fruit, too, because the Globe and Mail quoted a paragraph from it on page 9 of next morning's issue. At least, therefore, the broadcast was not made in vain.
I should like to sum up by saying the only purpose of this act is to protect the taxpayers of Canada. They look to the government to see that the vast sums of money appropriated for the defence of this country are properly spent. It has been my job, for 16 years, and it is still my job and will be my job, to see that my part of that responsibility is carried out properly. The act should be passed for that purpose and for no other purpose. If hon. members think that a greater purpose is served by protecting the defence manufacturers who are not asking for protection, then that is their business. In the meantime, in defending the legislation now before the house, I will do so with the conviction that I am working on the side of the angels.

The
minister who professes to be working on the side of the angels, Mr. Speaker, has just delivered himself of a speech which was, I suppose, the masterpiece of irrelevancy in

the experience of all hon. members sitting in this house today. I should like briefly to run down some of the things the minister has said this afternoon, just to indicate how completely they are amiss of the mark. This is a debate on second reading and we are supposed to be dealing with the principle of the bill we have before us. The amendment proposes that the bill be not now given second reading but that the subject matter of the bill be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce with certain directions to that committee.
But, sir, what do we And in the minister's speech this afternoon that was relevant to the principle of the bill, that principle being that the powers conferred upon the minister by this act should be made permanent? Let there be no doubt in the mind of any hon. member in this house, the very principle of this bill is that the powers conferred by the Defence Production Act upon a minister, not merely upon the government, shall be made permanent.
Now, what do we hear the minister saying? We hear the minister saying, first of all, that we have had powers comparable to these for a period of 16 years, less one year. Sir, what were the years and what were the conditions under which powers comparable to these were given? First, they were the war years; the years when the country was faced with the supreme emergency of all its history. Second, the several years immediately following the war, and then a state of emergency resulting from hostilities in Korea five years ago. Now, the minister is seeking to compare the conditions of today with those that obtained during the war and with those that obtained at the time of the emergency with respect to Korea. We will let that one stand on that basis. The minister's comparison is with the days of war, not with the days of peace.
The minister said today that the department cannot be made permanent without the Defence Production Act. Let us be a little more careful than the minister ever is about the subject under discussion. We are talking about this Defence Production Act. The minister knows quite well, and it has been said here time and again, although it does not seem to have seeped into his mind or into the minds of some hon. members opposite, that we have said there should be a permanent Department of Defence Production. Of course, that would require a Defence Production Act, but it would not require this Defence Production Act, loading as it does into the hands of the government and the
Defence Production Act minister powers that parliament has no right to give to a government or a minister in times like these.
Next, the minister said there have been no complaints from the people affected. He was referring, I suppose, to those manufacturers or suppliers or farmers, or anybody else who has any property that could be declared an essential material under the authority of this act. He says that none of these people have made complaints. Complaint has been made in this house, eloquent complaint very often by hon. members who have spoken here on behalf of the farmers and producers and all those Canadians who stand, so long as the powers continue under this act, with a sword of Damocles hanging over their heads, over their properties and over their rights. It is the Minister of Defence Production alone who, under this legislation, retains the power to say whether that sword shall or shall not fall. The minister says the people affected have not complained. Would you expect complaint from those who are doing business with the government, from those who are enjoying contracts at the hands of the Minister of Defence Production? Now, that was certainly a little too much to foist upon the credulity of even hon. members sitting opposite.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Surely the hon. member for Simcoe might have said something about it; he has had experience with the act.
The minister for Simcoe?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The hon. member for-
Chicago.
The minister is lost again.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: -Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson).

The minister is lost again. It is not only his geography that is wrong; it is his whole concept and approach to powers at the expense of parliament.
Now, I pass on to the next bogey that the minister whipped up to frighten the house today. He says we have unprecedented demands for nickel; we have unprecedented demands for copper. It was about time the minister said something about these metals because you will remember, when the resolution preceding this bill was before the house last March, it was the alleged shortage of nickel and the alleged shortage of copper that the minister used as the principal reason why the house should put these powers in his hands permanently. And he did not say a word when he introduced this measure

Defence Production Act several weeks ago on that subject. His silence on that occasion on this subject I think was more eloquent than anything he could have said on the subject. Sir, if there is this shortage, and if there are these threats of shortages of supplies, do you not think the minister would have had occasion to use this power which he says now is so necessary in his hands? The fact of the matter is, and the minister knows it, that it is not necessary to have power like this. The minister, even in the conditions he placed before the house this afternoon, when he sought to frighten the house, has not found it necessary to use these powers.
And, sir, I think we know very well by now that it was not any lack of love on the part of the minister for those powers that caused him to refrain from using them.
And the minister, who I see is now retiring from the house-
Good reason.

He may stay within earshot. I hope he will, because I have some things to say to him. It may be that the minister, like the Prime Minister, does not like debates when there is some criticism against him, and does not like people crossing him. Well, let me tell the minister that if he stays in this . House of Commons we will have something to say to him that will cross him.
And, Mr. Speaker, before we leave this subject of the alleged scarcities of nickel and copper, let me ask the minister-and he owes it to the House of Commons to say definitely -whether if these powers are continued in his hands he intends to make orders with respect to the supply and production and distribution of these metals.
The next bogey, the next irrelevancy, the next red herring dragged across the trail was what the minister said to us about the Orenda engine and the production of CF-lOO's. The minister said, or sought to leave the impression, that the production of Orenda engines and CF-100 aircraft required the powers conferred by this act, that those powers had been used and had been necessary. Sir, that is not a fact. That is not so. The minister cannot point to the use of any powers under this act in connection with the production of Orenda engines or CF-100 aircraft. And when he tries to build up a case this afternoon, talking about using these powers in connection with this program of supersonic aircraft, he is wrong and he knows it. It is not the power under this act that is going to be used in connection with that program; it is going to be the money of the taxpayers of Canada.
[Mr. Fleming.)

Then the next bogey, the next irrelevancy, the next red herring, was what the minister had to say about property and persons. He said this afternoon, "We have not the power under this act to touch persons. We have power only over property." Well, it is a pity the minister would not read his own act, of which he professed to be the draftsman, when it was introduced in 1951. Let him look at section 32 which says that power is given to create all kinds of sweeping orders under the act, and thereby create offences for breaches of the act. And if the minister will look at section 32 he will see that power is given there to impose penalties against persons for breaches of orders passed under the authority of the act. Those penalties are not confined to property. Under that section fines up to $5,000 and imprisonment can both be imposed as a penalty; and imprisonment up to two years. Does the minister now say that there is no power in the act over persons? The fact of the matter is that there are severe penalties for breaches of this act, or orders passed by the minister under the act.
Then, the next irrelevancy, the next red herring was that the minister said the time had now come when he must insist that this legislation be passed. Sir, let all hon. members in this house take due notice that the government is telling them that the time has now come when the government insists that they, the members of this house who are the sovereign representatives of the Canadian people, they the members of a sovereign Canadian parliament, must obey the government when it says that the time has come when they insist that this legislation be passed.
Is there any room left, in the face of a threat like that, for any hon. member who does not bow the knee to this all-powerful government? The government has cracked the whip; the government has given them their orders, and the orders have come from this source of all power, the Minister of Defence Production, who says that the time has now come when the parliament of Canada must pass this legislation.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I was not sent here by the people of my riding to bow the knee to any government passing out orders. And if I were an hon. member opposite, even if I had been elected to support this government, out of respect for the people who elected me and because of self-respect I would not yield to orders of that kind. I suggest to hon. members opposite that they should not yield to threats and coercion of that kind, and that they should remain true to the trust they were sent here to uphold, as members of the Canadian parliament, and should not accept orders from the government like that.

Then the minister finished up in a way that was designed to make all members melancholy and sad, and even to weep, by saying that his only purpose is to protect the taxpayer.
What is a million?

Well, that, coming from the Minister of Defence Production, does not mean very much, because if there is a man sitting in the House of Commons today who has shown more indifference in relation to the money of the taxpayer than has the Minister of Defence Production, I would like to know who it is.
But, sir, that is not the principal point I am offering in relation to this bill. This is the minister who said: "What is a million dollars?" -because it was nothing to him. Rather, I would draw the attention of the house to this fact, that the powers with which the minister is seeking to be invested permanently under this act are not required at all to protect the taxpayers of this country. They have not been used for that purpose. They were not sought for that purpose in the first place. They will not be used for that purpose. They are not needed for that purpose, because today we are in a buyers' market. The minister has said-it is on record-that he has no trouble getting businessmen now to agree to take defence contracts.
I am not sure yet whether he has support from the government or not; I would like to hear other members of the government tell us whether they are prepared to go as far as the minister wants us to go today. Let them get up and tell us. I would particularly like to hear the Prime Minister tell us. Let him tell us whether he supports what the Minister of Defence Production said here today.
What does it mean? This is the essence of what the minister says. He says they have a program of orders here, and that we must rely on the government; and therefore those who are summoned to rely upon the government are called upon to abdicate the powers of parliament and invest them in a certain man. That is the type of reliance this power-loving government demands on the part of its supporters, the kind of reliance that bids them yield up in the name of the parliament of Canada absolute power; that is the kind of reliance.
Parliament! What is parliament to the minister? Parliament is not even to be permitted to be a partner with this all-powerful government in working out this program of defence production. Bring these matters to parliament? Why, the idea is unthinkable to
Defence Production Act this government opposite. What is parliament, anyway? Parliament to them is but a nuisance. We have had proof abundant today, sir; all this talk, all this poppycock about parliament is just lip service from this allpowerful government opposite.
Sir, the issue remains precisely where we placed it at the opening of this debate several weeks ago. The time that has been spent will not have been misspent if there is on the part of hon. members or on the part of the people of Canada an understanding of the true issue involved in this debate.
There is abundant evidence that whether or not hon. members opposite have taken the trouble to read this bill, to think independently in relation to the government's demand for permanent power, the people of this country and the press of this country are seeing clearly the issue here involved. And that issue I say, sir, is whether sweeping, untrammelled, absolute powers should be made permanent in this government.
If hon. members regret that this debate is being protracted at this late stage of the session let them place the responsibility for it exactly where it belongs, on the head of the government and particularly on the head of the Prime Minister; for this matter was introduced in this house in the first week of March, three and one-half months ago. Sir, the resolution was dealt with then and it was at that time that the house was given assurance by the Prime Minister that the government would take another look at these powers before the matter was brought up again. They waited three long months until the house thought it was in the late stages of the session before they dared to bring back this measure and tell the house that they would submit to no diminution of those powers. I hope hon. members opposite object; I hope they dislike the way the business of this house is being cast about in order to meet the convenience of the government and to assist in satisfying this government's appetite for power.
Sir, there are some features of this debate that might well be commented upon. Those who have sat in this house with the Minister of Defence Production know that the real man speaks in moments of heat, in interjections, not in those manuscripts that are placed in his hands to read in the house. And that is one thing I would remind the house of when hon. members opposite see any reading done on this side of the house. Yes, it is in his unguarded moments, in moments of very free speaking, when we see the real man; for it will be remembered that "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speak-eth", and the mouth spoke at page 4542 of

Defence Production Act Hansard, but not in the way it is recorded in Hansard. If you will look at what the Minister of Defence Production said in an interjection you will see that it is watered down; it is a milk and water version:
When this emergency is through we may wish to liquidate this act. I do not propose to be told now by any hon. member just when X will liquidate it.
These are not the words that were uttered by the minister in this house. I was struck by those words, and I made a note of them at that time. I checked afterwards and found that changes were made before Hansard was printed. What was said then was this:

I think we all regretted very much the remarks made by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). I regret that he is not here today, and I am sure all hon. members regret the occasion which calls him home and hope that his aged father will recover his health. In the speech he made last week the hon. member completely missed the point. It was a great disappointment to hear that speech coming from the hon. member for Spadina. He said in effect that it was enough
Defence Production Act that the minister had agreed that there would be a further amendment introduced to this bill to provide that when orders were made, not only would they be published in the Canada Gazette but they would be tabled in the house with the provision that if any ten members so requested there would be a debate.
The hon. member for Spadina and other hon. members know perfectly well that the moment that happens it becomes a question of confidence in the government. We have had occasions when Liberal members in the house have taken one stand and then in effect have voted the other way because they said it amounted to a question of confidence in the government. The hon. member is saying that it is a sufficient maintenance of the parliamentary system that wide powers should be given to a minister to legislate, provided that after he has exercised those powers some power is given to the House of Commons to discuss what he has done, after the fact. When did parliament become reduced to that position? When did it become a proper maintenance of parliamentary principles and the parliamentary institutions which we are sworn to uphold here to give power to this minister to legislate, and then after it is all over parliament's contact with the matter will be sufficient if parliament is permitted to discuss it after the legislation is passed? It is not merely that this should be done in connection with what might be called emergency legislation; it is that this should be done in connection with legislation that now becomes a permanent part of the statute law of Canada. If it is considered good enough in connection with the Department of Defence Production, if this act becomes permanent, then it may be considered good enough in relation to the exercise by parliament of any power it possesses in giving or delegating legislation to the minister or the government to be used in that way.
Apparently that is good enough to satisfy the consciences of hon. members opposite. But this is not temporary legislation; this now becomes permanent legislation. The powers are permanent. Let no hon. member approach this as though it were simply upon the basis of an emergency. There are many proofs that there is no emergency.

We now ask if the minister has made a commitment under the powers given to him by section 15(f). If not, is he going to? These are proper questions and they should be answered. It would be well to know if other members of the cabinet were taken into the confidence of the minister in connection with any such exercise of these sweeping and broad powers.
What we have here are all the elements for a dictatorship. Here are also all the elements necessary to foist socialism upon this country. Here are also the elements required to permit the constitution of this country to be trampled upon. How otherwise can you explain powers such as those conferred by section 28, which gives the cabinet 
the power to override by order the application of any statute and any obligation created by statute or contract? These are the powers conferred upon this minister, and constitutionally they could never be supported except on the basis of the existence of an emergency. There is nothing in the statute law of Canada today declaring an emergency. There is nothing in this bill that declares an emergency. There is nothing that can legally support giving these sweeping and untrammelled powers on the basis of the existence of a national emergency. The fact is that last year, when it permitted the Emergency Powers Act to expire, parliament eliminated the last parliamentary declaration of the existence of a national emergency which would have permitted the federal jurisdiction to override provincial jurisdiction under the constitution.
The issue remains. It is the issue of parliamentary control. Shall it be made a part of the permanent statutory law of Canada that the government-and in most cases the minister alone-shall take powers from parliament and shall not come back to parliament? Why all this unwillingness to come to parliament? Why all this unwillingness to have these matters discussed in parliament? Is parliament not responsible? Is parliament not even to enjoy the confidence of the minister? Is parliament not to be told anything? Is parliament simply to be ignored, as though we should not be permitted to discuss matters as important as national defence? If this government had a correct attitude toward parliament it would encourage interest and participation by hon. members of this house in all matters relating to defence production.
This then becomes an issue of the unwillingness of the government to take parliament into its confidence, to permit parliament to have any part in the discussion of matters pertaining to national defence and defence production. In no other way can the attempt, the palpable, open, brazen attempt of the government to by-pass parliament in this matter be explained.

Mr. Speaker, press reports during the last few days have described what we are trying to do here in the House of Commons as "Her Majesty's loyal opposition conducting a filibuster". This word "filibuster" has been borrowed from the dictionary by our neighbours to the south and given a colloquial meaning. If we have conducted a filibuster we are proud of it, because what we are trying to do, as the minister knows, is fight against the permanent powers in the Defence Production Act.

I believe we have done what we set out to do, which was to awaken the people to what is going on here in parliament, and awaken them to the encroachment on our freedoms and liberties. The press across Canada has commended our stand in editorials, in news columns and cartoons; and the people of Canada-or, to use the minister's words today, the peasants-have understood what we are trying to do, that we are trying to stop this power from being given to one man and being put in our statutes permanently.
As the hon. member for Eglinton said, it was with a great deal of interest and surprise that we listened to the hon. member for Spadina the other day. It was with interest because he is practically the only government member who has spoken on this bill, and it was with surprise because all across Canada he has won a reputation for great liberalism, with a small "1"; and he is a man well known for his championship of the rights of the people. Yet in this battle for the rights of parliament, which is the voice of the people, the hon. member for Spadina said the people of Canada could not care less about this issue because there is no issue. He said that as far as the government is concerned our arguments have fallen on deaf ears but not on closed minds.
I believe the hon. member was wrong in his interpretation. I agree with the Globe and Mail editorial of the other day which said that this debate is one of the most important that has taken place in parliament for a long time. It is very difficult to understand why so many voices are silent on the government side-silent or silenced. The yes men, with their deaf ears and open minds, have been singularly quiet. I believe they may well have some difficulty explaining to the people they represent here in parliament why they were so silent while the rights of parliament were being whittled away.
We on this side are not quite so surprised that the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) has been conspicuous by his absence from this debate. He also is recognized as a man of great liberalism. It is with considerable surprise that we find that the hon. member for Durham (Mr. James) should sit silent in this debate, as he comes from a section of Canada that throughout our history has stood for responsible government and for the sovereignty of parliament.
I think a good many of us on this side of the house were surprised when the hon. member for Spadina spoke, because we could not accept his claim to have an open mind. It seemed to us that he was downright obtuse. He said we cannot afford to relax or drop our guard. We say that is true. He said we
Defence Production Act cannot afford to be unprepared. We say that is true. He paid tribute to those on this side of the house who have served their country well and, he said, some gloriously. He said he was sure they would be the first to demand that such services be supported by a department of government with power. We say that is true too, in wartime. We are certainly not suggesting in any way that we relax or drop our guard. We are not suggesting that we allow ourselves to become unprepared.
The minister says these powers are necessary at this time. We say, "All right; take these powers at this time, but not for all time". We do not object to the powers, but we do object to the permanent powers. When the Defence Production Act was brought in, in 1951, a time limit was set. The Prime Minister said at that time that there was no particular significance to the date named, July 31, 1956, as the date the Defence Production Act would expire. On March 2, 1951, the Prime Minister said that there was no particular significance to this date other than to recognize that some of the powers sought in this bill are special powers which should not be continuing powers.
We say the Prime Minister spoke truly on that day in 1951. There certainly was no particular significance to the date, as we realize now on June 28, 1955. In fact, that date of July 31, 1956, was so insignificant we are now being asked to brush it aside completely by this clause:
Section 41 of the said act is repealed.
No hon. member in this debate has denied that the Minister of Defence Production likes power. He has not denied it himself. Nor are we of the opposition trying in any way to deny him the power he wants. We have repeated it many times, all of us on this side of the house, though we seem to be making no headway. The fact of the matter is that giving the power to the minister whenever he needs it is quite agreeable to us, but not for all time.
No matter how often we repeat this, the sense of it does not seem to penetrate. It falls on deaf ears and on closed minds. What we object to is the desire for permanent powers. We feel that therein lies a tyranny that must be stopped.
It is true we cannot stop the minister. If he wants to do anything he can get away with it, but certainly not before we have had our say. History, both ancient and modern, has shown that tyranny is not something that just bursts upon civilization suddenly. It is a slow process. It is a whittling away of our

Defence Production Act liberties until there is no liberty left. Once established, that tyranny or power pushes its roots deep until it is wellnigh impossible to uproot it.

I call attention to one such profound truth found in Hansard of June 8, at page 4557. The hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) had made some pertinent points about the way dictatorships arise, and the remarks seemed to annoy the minister. The passage reads:
... I have not said what X have just said for the pleasure of annoying the minister or any other member of the government. If I happen to be annoying them-

Ten minutes is not long when you are trying to kill off a parliament.
It seems to me that interjection is the reason for this so-called filibuster of ours. We are trying to stop the killing off of parliament. The senior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) had some comments to make about what he called our inconsistency on this side of the house. He could not understand how the Conservatives could express appreciation of the minister's business ability and yet be so concerned about his greed for power. As found at page 4689 of Hansard of June 13, the senior member for Halifax said:
It is beyond me how he and other members can in one breath express the greatest confidence in the Minister of Defence Production and refer to his tremendous record of achievement in this country-
I think these adjectives are a slight exaggeration.
__then in the very next breath attack the same
minister and express the greatest concern about his powers, saying that he is an autocrat, that he is moved only by a lust and a desire for power.
Our concern, Mr. Speaker, is not so much the minister himself or even the powers. As we have said again and again, it is the permanency of these powers. The Minister of Defence Production is not infallible. We know he is impatient with the slow pace of parliament. We also know he is nearing the end of his political career and will soon take a well earned rest. What will happen then? We are being asked to give these powers for all time to some man now unknown. No matter who he is, no one man should have such permanent powers in a democracy.
In a speech recently my leader listed these powers in a way that brings out most forcefully the dangers in the Prime Minister's
[Miss Aitken.l
bill to make these extraordinary powers permanent. The Leader of the Opposition said: It would give a single minister, without even the formality of an order in council, power to seize any business, large or small; to cancel contracts; to take over any material that the minister thinks could be used in the production of defence requirements; to control professional and other personal services; to manufacture and process any defence supplies; to purchase, sell, rent or otherwise acquire or dispose of any real or personal property which in the opinion of the minister alone is likely to be necessary or desirable for these purposes; and to make loans or advances to any person for the purpose of doing all these things. As if these powers, to be exercised without even consulting the government, let alone parliament, were not enough, the act provides that the minister may "do all such things as appear to the minister to be incidental to or necessary or expedient" to the carrying out of all these extraordinary powers. In addition to these the minister has power to demand information about any detail of the business of any company or individual capable of producing defence supplies.
When the minister spoke he said he had no complaints from the people engaged in defence production. Earlier in this debate mention was made of a fear compulsion. If he has had no complaint I think it is probably because of that fear compulsion. He claims that the freedom of the individual is protected; yet there are these sinister words about controllers and investigators being appointed whenever the minister thinks it necessary.
The Winnipeg Free Press has called the demands of the Minister of Defence Production silly. We call these demands for power downright evil in a democracy. We shall continue to fight them as long as the machinery of parliament allows us to try to save parliament itself. We believe that you cannot defeat any enemy, whether it be communism or any other "ism", by betraying our own liberties and freedoms.
Mr. W. M. Hamilton (Notre Dame de
Grace): Mr. Speaker, by the amendment it is proposed to refer the bill to the banking and commerce committee. In the light of the discussion we have heard in the house this afternoon, I think that is a very sound and worth-while suggestion. Such a committee would be in a position to call witnesses before it. For example, we could hear those who are engaged in executive positions in defence industry itself. We could hear what they have to say. There has been some suggestion, and I think it is founded in fact, that the executives of large defence industries throughout the country would otherwise think twice before they would put themselves in the position of criticizing or objecting to government policies when the government is one of their best customers.

We could have representatives of individual labour unions appear before the committee. We could hear what they have to say. But I think perhaps best of all we might have the opportunity to discuss the details of this measure with the Minister of Defence Production. That might give us an opportunity to put various points before him and hear his minute observations. It is difficult for the Minister of Defence Production to deal with these things in a regular debate of this kind where he can speak only once. It would be easy for him to do so in the committee, and perhaps might be helpful to the house as a whole when the report of the committee was made.
I hope the Minister of Defence Production will take note of these remarks. He will have to read them in Hansard, because he is not here, but then neither are 19 of his colleagues. The fort is being held by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham). I do not know what close interest he has in this, but I am certainly glad there is at least one minister who has sufficient interest in this important bill to remain in his seat in the house.
I think perhaps too in that committee we might hear from some of the government supporters who have been so notably quiet in this debate. There may be some of them who feel they have made their remarks for this year. But I do think some of these hon. members who have not spoken for one year, two years, three years, might like to appear before the committee and give us the benefit of their observations. I believe that in the informality of that committee we might bring forth facts which it is difficult to bring forth here in the house.
I feel that referring such an important matter as this to a committee might be a gain for the committee system of this house. In thinking about it, I looked up one of the standard references on the government of Canada by Dawson, which in fact bears that name, and here is what he says at page 412:
While the standing committees are frequently impressive they are. in fact, not a very important part of the legislative machinery. From time to time one or more of the committees may be very busy and perhaps extremely useful, but their activity is sporadic and uncertain.
I suggest that the reference of this measure to such a committee would perhaps, if that is necessary, point up the importance of committees in the work of this house. I do not agree, Mr. Speaker, with the definition of a committee which I saw at one time, and which reads:
A group of the unfit appointed by the unwilling to do the unnecessary.
