I would hope that a committee of this house would be very fit. The government may be unwilling, but certainly we are not, to take our part in it. Certainly a review of this measure is vitally necessary. I think the results would be something different from those envisaged by another definition of a committee, which reads:
A group of people who individually can do nothing, but who meet collectively to agree unanimously that nothing can be done.
This is something that can be done about this measure. This is something which is very simple, and which is the exact opposite of the stand taken by the minister this afternoon. It reflects the realization that those who are on this side of the house are quite willing-call it by whatever term you like, filibuster or delaying action-to accept their democratic responsibilities, and will use every means in their power to see that this measure is brought back down to earth and has a time limit put on it. There are those of us here who accept those responsibilities. In that committee we might be able to examine in some detail the actual responsibilities of this Department of Defence Production.
This afternoon the minister, in attempting to inject humour into his speech-he did get a chuckle out of it-mentioned a reference of mine to the Department of Defence Production and nylon stockings and underwear. He said that reference might have been the result of the heat. Well, Mr. Speaker, it was not the result of the heat. I find myself in very good company in that respect because in the annual report of his department for 1954 there is a chart showing some of the things that department must purchase. I mentioned nylon underwear, and someone mentioned nylon stockings. His own report mentioned musical instruments, chapel equipment, packaging and recreational equipment.
As a matter of fact, let us just run very quickly down the list to see the extent of the things which are lumped under this measure as defence supplies. They are hardware, tools, fire fighting and safety equipment, electrical equipment, electrical wire and cable, motors, generators, lighting, heating and cooking equipment-that would be stoves-medical, pharmaceutical, dental, optical, laboratory, hospital, photographic supplies and equipment, scientific instruments, metals, metal fabrication, plumbing, heating, air conditioning equipment, hose and rubber products generally. That is general supplies division No. 1.
Then general supplies division No. 2 is concerned with the following: food and catering services, fuel, petroleum products, chemicals, alcohol, gases, soaps, cleansers, waxes,

Defence Production Act polishes, disinfectants, insecticides, kitchen and messing equipment-the minister has messed around with this enough now that you would not think he had to have a section in his own department to do more messing- cooling and refrigeration equipment, paints, brushes, scales, adhesives, special projects (general); furniture, lumber, wood products, paper and paper products, packaging, recreational equipment, musical instruments, chapel equipment.
Then general supplies division No. 3 is concerned with vehicles, motor transport, spare parts and accessories; tires and tubes, repair and overhaul-all commodities-industrial road building and maintenance equipment, ground handling-that is probably the department that looks after landscaping-garage equipment, batteries.
The last one is the clothing and textiles division, which is concerned with uniforms, fatigue and Arctic clothing, headwear, inner clothing, knit goods, rubber and leather products, textiles, bedding and canvas goods- then this interesting little classification-buttons, badges, buckles, requirements planning of clothing and textiles, cloth warehousing. All these things come under the purview of this department. I retreat not one step from my observation with regard to nylon underwear, which also comes under his department.
Then this afternoon the minister attempted to suggest to the house-I think I have his observation here-that they did not need the act for ordinary supply purchasing, but it was needed for weapons. In his report for 1952 we find this statement:
Recognizing that the sustaining of a sound mobilization base must include support for many segments of the economy which are auxiliary to defence, the department continued to provide priorities assistance on materials and equipment in such important fields as agriculture, power development, communications and transportation, as well as channelling supplies into direct defence activities.
In the face of that statement appearing over the signature of the minister who rose in the house and spoke to us this afternoon, can he attempt to leave the impression with this house that the only reason for this act is for straight defence production and straight defence supplies, and that he does not plan or does not at the present time do, through the aegis of this department, work in fields which are by no means directly connected with defence production?
This committee might well consider the question of the permanency of the department. We on this side of the house are in agreement with the minister that the department should be permanent. The interesting thing is, Mr. Speaker, that even his own

report two years ago was not in agreement with that. In 1952 his report said:
In Canada a special temporary department was formed to supervise major and involved problems of the preparedness program and to handle the procurement of defence supplies.
Here we have the minister himself saying two years ago that this is only a temporary operation. Now he comes to the house and, forsaking all that which he told us in the past, forsaking his word of 1951, and forsaking the observations in his own report, asks that this entire act be made definitely permanent.
Then again, why was this department set up in the first place? For that again I turn to his report of 1952 and I find the minister
saying:
Establishment of the Department of Defence Production on April 1, 1951, was predicated-
Notice that word.
-predicated upon the fact that free nations of the world were living in danger of the international situation exploding into all-out war at any time.
I would ask the minister this. Does he feel that the situation is still exactly the same as it was in 1951? Unless he does feel that international affairs are still in that tremendously uneasy state, then the basis upon which this department was predicated has very largely disappeared at the present time.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we have the question of the function of the department in relation to the Canadian economy, which would be envisioned as one of the subjects to be discussed by this committee. When the department was set up its first report said:
The Defence Supplies Act provided the minister with basic powers to carry out the procurement functions with which he was charged, but was not considered adequate to meet the situation which resulted from the decision to embark on a substantially expanded defence program. Accordingly the Defence Production Act, which was modelled in large measure on the Department of Munitions and Supply Act, was enacted to provide special powers to the minister to the end that requirements of defence should be met in priority to other demands on available supply.
In other words let me emphasize that the Defence Supplies Act was not considered adequate at that time to meet the situation which resulted from the decision to embark upon a substantially expanded defence program. And that is borne out throughout the minister's report. Later on in the 1951 report he said the government had embarked upon a three-year program designed to increase and strengthen Canada's defence effort, and that this program was going to increase our production potential. Then later in the report he pointed out how the government was faced with the problem of meeting

an expanded defence program with an economy which was already operating at full steam, when there were many shortages of materials, and when the world demand for materials was steadily increasing.
In the light of those facts in 1951 let us see what the minister and his department have seen fit to say subsequently. In 1952 he told us-
-the program now well under way with many production facilities in operation and with a steady delivery of defence orders for practically all phases of the program.
And later in the same report:
Much of the new production is flowing from Canadian facilities which did not exist when the department was established.
And later, under the heading "Material Situation Improves" he said:
An important development during the year was the improving raw material supply. The improvement in the supply situation was particularly true of the basic materials produced in Canada.
That sounds odd to me, in the light of the plea this afternoon about our shortage of nickel and copper and other commodities, when back in 1952 our supplies situation was improving so well. Then in 1953, and again I am quoting the minister's words-
As the supply position of strategic materials continued to improve it was possible to reduce Canadian controls.
Then he deals with certain changes in operations, and certain restrictions. In that year they closed down the small industries division offices outside of Ottawa, and so far as I can see from the present organizational chart the small industries division does not now exist at all. In his 1953 report he gives us a glowing picture of the achievements of the Canadian defence industry. It is obvious that he is very happy about it.
Then in 1954 we come to the point at which the minister demonstrates that the department seems to have achieved the initial objective it set out to reach. He' says:
The initial build-up of the country's defence potential was largely completed during the past year and, in line with the long-term needs of the armed forces, the emphasis was shifted to the scheduling of production to meet a continuing high level of defence procurement.
And later in the same report:
The major facilities required for the production in Canada of larger quantities of a greater variety of defence items had been established by the beginning of 1954. Defence industries had no difficulty during the year in obtaining their necessary requirements of essential materials and skilled manpower and no domestic controls were required.
Yet the same man this afternoon would have left anyone listening to his speech, and not knowing the facts, with the impression that these controls were needed because of the imminent shortages in Canada.
Defence Production Act
Now we have the question of the change in attitude of the minister. And, just as an aside in this connection, in the minister's remarks this afternoon he omitted to point out that the production of nickel and copper is at the highest level this country has ever known. Where, oh where, oh where is the justification for the crocodile tears which were shed in those two particular fields this afternoon by the minister? I do not know what else sheds crocodile tears, Mr. Speaker, and I shall not search for a word.
Then, turning to the change in attitude of the department towards its functions, we find that in the last four years that attitude has changed substantially. When the department was initiated, when the minister was set up in this business, it was a temporary proposition. Above all, the powers were temporary. As late as his own report for 1952 he was talking about a temporary department. Now nothing will do but that every measure, every power and every iota of control which this act vests in the minister must be perpetuated for all time to come. I am no expert on musical comedy, but there are many other fields than musical comedy in which the expression "all or nothing" has been used. I suggest that this is yet another case in which the ultimate desire of the minister is encompassed in those three little words, "all or nothing".
We on our part are prepared to give the minister something. We are not unreasonable; we are not standing here and suggesting that he wants all but we will not give him anything. There is a middle ground; there is a reasonable ground, and it is that ground which we have been trying to reach. It is that ground which we are being deprived of by the strong and unreasonable position the minister is taking.
We find again, Mr. Speaker, that the department's attitude has changed. It is changing from special powers for priority in defence supplies to a permanent organization which does not particularly need those powers, but which wants to hold them in the unlikely event that they will be used for ordinary procurement for the armed forces. And that is the comparison; special powers for priority in 1951; today special powers for ordinary procurement for the armed forces.
In 1951 the government may have needed the Defence Production Act to meet their defence requirements and priorities. They did say at that time that the Defence Supplies Act was not considered adequate to meet the situation which resulted from the decision to

Defence Production Act embark on a substantially expanded defence program. But in 1954 we find the report of the department saying:
The need was not so much one of producing a large volume of weapons and other military equipment in the shortest possible time, but rather one of obtaining immediate requirements and of creating production potential that could be greatly expanded on short notice.
Compare these two phrases which I have drawn to your attention, Mr. Speaker. In 1951 we were asked to support this measure on the grounds that the government was embarking on a substantially expanded defence program. In 1954 the department's report tells us that they are creating production potential that could be greatly expanded on short notice. Actually what they have done is to change the rules completely in the middle of the game just to find some justification for the continuation of these powers. In 1951 they were planning an expansion of the Canadian industrial economy, particularly in the field of defence production. They claimed they needed the powers for that reason. They were given those powers; they operated on those powers, and they achieved that expansion. Now, in 1955, having achieved their ends but being unwilling to relinquish their powers, they try to justify their continuation on a totally new basis and one which is completely foreign to the need for those particular powers.
I turn just for a moment or two, Mr. Speaker, to one or two of the observations of the minister this afternoon. One which particularly disturbed me a great deal was his suggestion that he was bothered by having $30 or $40 million of Canadian money invested in some operation that might go bad. The reason that statement disturbed me is that it seemed to indicate that the minister had progressed from his position of several years ago when he said, "What's a million dollars?" Now, apparently, in order to disturb the minister he must have $30 or $40 million of public money invested in some enterprise or some defence production undertaking. You must have $30 or $40 million involved before you can get the minister to lie awake nights and worry about it.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada might be better served if they had a group of men on the treasury benches who were perturbed and worried not when it came to $30 or $40 million, but when it came to $3,000 or $4,000, and who paid some attention to financial expenditures that were within reason, small expenditures they could control, as well as the big expenditures.
Certainly I am not suggesting for a moment that the minister should not be perturbed

over $30 or $40 million. I think he should; I think we all would; but I do suggest to you that he would be well advised to come down a little and realize that there are many other expenditures in his department which are equally important if not equally large.
When the minister was speaking on the question of individual liability under this act and whether the individual was protected he made the remark-certainly this is the sense of it, if not his exact words-that it was a good defence in law to say that the action was not necessary for the defence of Canada. In some of my earlier remarks I related the operations of this department to such things as belts, buckles, musical instruments, recreational equipment, and many other equally unlikely objects in the field of defence production. This indicates that it would be small defence indeed, if any, to say that the case being complained about was not necessary for the defence of Canada, because the minister himself has shown by his own report that just about everything in this great and growing economy of ours is connected and concerned with the defence of Canada.
And, then, of course-I hardly need emphasize it-there was his sanguine observation that no one to his knowledge among the defence production industries had come to him and complained about the powers contained in this act. When we see the day that a mouse comes along and without any defence whatsoever calls upon the cat and complains about the way in which the cat is exercising its powers, then we may expect the defence industries to protest to the minister. Certainly at the present time I think it would be a cause for tremendous surprise if the minister received complaints from his suppliers. It just does not happen that way.
I do not think there was one word uttered by the minister this afternoon which was truly germane to the issue which has been placed before us so clearly by this bill. Certainly Canadian industry is doing a good job in defence production. Certainly we are proud of Canadian industry. Certainly if you have $30 or $40 million invested in some enterprise which may or may not turn out all right you are going to worry. Certainly there has been some form of control over munitions and supplies for 16 years. Certainly there have been shortages in the past. I could go on, but I shall not.
But equally certainly this is not a question to be decided on the grounds of the minister's observations this afternoon. This is not a question of expediency; this is not a question of administration; this is nothing except the main, basic and fundamental

concept of freedom in a democracy. This is the conflict between genuine freedom in which parliament will decide as against the bogus freedom in which the minister will decide and then parliament be told what he has decided. There can be many more speeches from the government benches, there can be many defences on the same grounds as those advanced by the minister, but they will not be defences having to do with the basic issue as we on this side see it.
I await the day, and it will be a glorious day for freedom, when one person on the government side stands up and says, "I have examined this bill, I have listened to the arguments for and against it, and in the light of those arguments I am going to put aside my party allegiance and vote in the interests of the people of Canada and against this bill. I am going to do what I can to protect and further the cause of freedom". On that day and on that day alone will I know there is some life and some sense of responsibility left in the ranks of those who sit opposite and those who encumber the benches to my right; those who at this moment stand for nothing which is in the cause of freedom but for everything which would destroy freedom and reduce us gradually but surely to a controlled and largely dictatorial state.

Mr. Speaker, there is a saying that the Campbells are coming, and perhaps today the Hamiltons are coming. Since I spoke last in this debate I have been trying to find some basic point or points on which the minister might have anchored his position, which would make his desire for this legislation more understandable. I listened carefully to what he had to say today, but I was unable to enlighten myself as to the true background for those reasons. In the ordinary course of events I think we can take each reason in turn, as I did once before, and examine it to see if it provides some basis for this legislation. I have been unable to find any reason for this hidebound adherence to the proposed legislation, and have come to the conclusion that the reason for this legislation is tied up inexplicably with the minister's mental outlook.
What we are battling here is not really a sound argument based on facts and logical forecasts, but a psychological block in one man's mind. It is a difficult and illusory type of problem which we must diagnose and then attack. If this were a case before a criminal court I think I would be saying at this juncture that the crown's case was in. If I were acting as adequate defence counsel I would move for dismissal because there was no evidence to support the charge.
Defence Production Act

There is no necessity in a case of this kind in a court of law for the defence to produce evidence. The crown has failed to make its case. But I would say this, that it would be difficult for us to get the necessary evidence. The minister himself has said he has heard no complaints by those who produce for his department. Perhaps I might be able to repeat one saying, that this is a "don't quote me" department. We would mot expect that those who deal directly with this department would come forward and go into

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that was the shortest dinner hour I have had in a long time. In attempting to understand the almost unprecedented tenacity with which the government is holding on to this legislation, I repeat that I have been unable to find any basic reason given by the minister or by anyone else to support this stand.
Every indication is that industry today seeks contracts from the government. The textile industry was referred to earlier. The electronics industry is looking hopefully to the development of the defence warning lines and the St. Lawrence seaway as sources of business to keep their workmen on the job. We can go right down the list to the aircraft industry, to which the minister referred at great length in his arguments on the amendment. If I understand the situation correctly, the sole customer of the company to which he referred today, the A. V. Roe company, is his own department. Whether or not the production lines of that plant continue to operate rests wholly upon his own decision. Surely then it is not necessary for him to have such all-powerful legislation at his fingertips. These people are entirely dependent upon him now. His every decision, I am sure, is reflected in the program which is being carried out at that plant today.
The amendment proposed does not in fact remove from the minister the powers he now possesses and which were granted to him at a time of real emergency. The act as it stands

continues these powers until next year. The amendment simply provides an opportunity for a complete study of the type of powers which should be made available in a new kind of peacetime. These may be the only ordinary peaceful times in which we will live during our lifetime. Peace as we knew it from 1918 until 1939 may never again come about. We must adapt ourselves to this new type of peace through strength, for it is the only peace we will know.
I suggest that since the programs I have referred to, documented in the minister's own report, indicate that the peak has been reached and that a levelling off is now taking place at figures which will ensure the adequate protection of the country, there is now no need to continue this emergency legislation. I say again, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment placed before you by the official opposition does not, today, tomorrow or the next day, remove from the minister the powers he possesses at the present time. He will still be able to carry on until the house convenes again, and I am quite satisfied that in the interim proper wording for legislation of this kind can be produced by the legal officers of the crown to ensure not only that the country will be able to maintain adequate protection but that the freedom of the individual will also be protected.
The minister says that persons are not affected by the act. I do not wish to repeat the argument of the hon. member for Eglin-ton, but I say to the minister that if all properties are controllable by the act then, no matter what else is said, the persons who are involved with those properties are in fact personally controlled. It has often been said that the sole power of the government is based on its power to tax. If that be true, then I say that the power in the minister's hands to control all things connected with the defence effort does in fact mean control of the people themselves.
Therefore I would ask, as did the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, that those who sit opposite think twice about this legislation. There is a course that can be followed which will ensure not only protection for the country but freedom for the individual.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to the amendment, with which I find myself in complete accord, I am amazed at the spectacle this debate has created in the house. As I listened this afternoon I must say I was very proud of my colleagues and their contributions to the debate. Amidst the silence of the government, with the exception of gibes and heckling, you have heard from the junior members of our [DOT]50433-341
Defence Production Act party excellent speeches, all sound and logical; so sound, I believe, that the silence of the government would almost indicate that they have no logical answer to these speeches. I say that, Mr. Speaker, in all sincerity.
I say this is a spectacle such as I have not witnessed in the house in the last quarter of a century, that a proposal so important as this, and one that has aroused the interest of the press all over this country, that has stirred the imagination of junior members and has agitated senior members-except those who are admirers and trained supporters of the government-should be debated at length in these hot and tedious days of the last part of the session. I have not before witnessed anything quite the same.
This afternoon we heard from the Minister of Defence Production, for whom I have a keen personal regard. He laboured and floundered in his speech in such a way as to almost make one believe that he did not believe himself. It may have been because he had no support around him from the balance of his cabinet. It may have been that he was playing a lone hand, as he is seeking the power to do. I do not know, but I thought that lurking behind his statements was the almost silent conviction through his clear-headed logic that he was like the Irishman who had a wildcat by the tail and dare not let go, yet he was almost afraid to hang on.

I say with the utmost sincerity that I have a responsibility as a member of this house. I have a responsibility to parliament, to my riding and to myself. I dare not sit silent in my place on this issue. I have remained silent on many other issues. Sometimes when I listened to some of the debates I have felt that enough had been said, and at other times I thought too much had been said. I have never been one who employed the time of the house to lengthen the session of parliament unduly.
There is no one in this house who would rather end this session of parliament, feeling we had done our duty, more than I would. I have other interests and I have other enjoyments. I have other things I would prefer to be doing now than labouring to the empty benches on the government side.

Is there anyone within the sound of my voice who has ever seen a spectacle like this in parliament, when the Prime Minister who moved this motion three months ago and who said he was going to consider any possible changes in it, has failed to rise in this house during this protracted debate and explain his position?

It is the most neutralized thing I have ever seen come into parliament, and nobody is going to support it. It is the Prime Minister's bill and it is the Prime Minister's responsibility. Therefore the Prime Minister's silence was never more conspicuous, and his absence is even more conspicuous. It shows how parliament can be ignored.
I sat here this afternoon and listened to the Minister of Defence Production, who was supported by one lone minister. Even that minister was reading a paper and was so discouraged he wondered, "Where do we go from here?" They look over their position and they say, like Job, we may be wrong, hut how long, oh how long is this going to keep up? We do not like keeping it up, but we know it is our duty. We know the Prime Minister is out of the house. We know he observes silence on his own bill. We know it is his responsibility. We ask, why is it that he is not 100 per cent in accord with the measure?
Are the Prime Minister and the cabinet ministers indicating that they do not like it? Is the rumour in the corridors and in the press of this country that they are not in full accord with the Minister of Defence Production true? for temporary relief in an emergency, or is it an expedient to gain permanent power? Has anyone known of any emergency that needed more than temporary power? It looks to me more like an expedient. There is no possible justification for making this permanent. Even these little hecklers won't rise and say the minister should have these powers forever. As the hon. member for Halton (Miss Bennett) said today, and said so eloquently, "How freedom falls!"

He should be the last man in Canada who should initiate proceedings to make temporary powers permanent. Temporary powers have been sought and they have been granted. But always they have been limited. Now we have this new scarecrow. Is this house to be frightened into granting unlimited powers permanently at a time when no one can say honestly that we are in more difficult times than we were two years ago?
As was so well said today by the hon. member for Royal, and as has been pointed out and accepted by every member who can read the papers, the truth is that the situation throughout the world has improved. We are very glad about that, pray God it may continue. We all know very well that there are grave dangers and that there have been grave dangers. But why does the minister want these powers permanently? Is there any 50433-341i
Defence Production Act member in this House of Commons who would kiss the Bible and take the oath of allegiance to this country, and who at the same time would refuse powers to the Minister of Defence Production if he needed those powers? If the enemy were at our gates tomorrow morning, would those powers be refused? Why, Mr. Speaker, it is utterly nonsensical, it is ridiculous, it is absolutely absurd to suggest any such thing.
For so many years I listened to the former prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, talk about the supremacy of parliament. He said, "We Liberals trust the people of Canada; we trust parliament. Parliament should know everything." He would never declare war without parliament, would never even think of helping the mother country until he submitted it to parliament. "I stand by the supremacy of parliament, like my old grandfather", as he said at one time in the House of Commons.
But what a change there has been in a few years. Now parliament is more or less held in contempt. Parliament has been ignored. Who is asking us now to disregard parliament? Who is asking us to give power to make orders in council? It is the government that ruled this country for so many years by orders in council, this government that passed orders in council while parliament was sitting, when the matters could well have been placed before the House of Commons.
And now they go one step further. They ask us to give all this power to one man so he will not even be responsible to cabinet, let alone to parliament. And he says, "Oh, yes, but these powers can be revoked by me. Trust me to revoke them. Trust me not to invoke them." These are powers that can be invoked at any time, in any way, for any purpose, and by any minister who may hold the job at any time he believes there is any kind of a situation that he could call an emergency.
Mr. Speaker, the remaining members might as well go home. Even the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who speaks so often in parliament, would be of no avail, though he supports the measure. The rest of parliament may think the minister's actions are for political expediency, or for the expediency of the government, but despite all that the minister can do almost anything he likes. He can go to any private business, so long as he thinks what they are doing has been connected in any way at any time with defence production.
Mr. Speaker, where is the evidence that this power is needed? Where is the evidence that the emergency is worse than it was two

Defence Production Act years ago? Where is the evidence that it is worse than it was when they said it could be revoked in 1956? What power could be needed between now and the middle of next year that they do not have?
Why all this hurry? Why not do what was suggested by the Winnipeg Free Press, whose pronouncements are taken more or less as the watchword of those who sit to your right? Why not drop the bill at this time? Why not drop the bill when it is not needed? Why not return to a position where you trust the people of Canada? Has this party to your left, Mr. Speaker-this party which by its silence the government seems to want to ignore or hold in contempt-at any time, in wartime or at a time of national emergency, refused to play the game loyally in the interests of Canada? If there should be a war emergency again, then I say there is not one member from any district of Canada who would dare to refuse for one moment the granting of powers for which the Minister of Defence Production would ask, and would not grant them just as quickly as they were asked for.
Therefore I say that is not the issue. We do not know who may be in office in future. I do think there could be worse than the present minister. I would have been disappointed if the minister had not heard me, even if he was not listening. In the course of his remarks he said he was not going to be told by me or by anybody else when he was going to revoke this measure. In other words he suggested that we should not oppose it, and that when he wanted to revoke it he would do so whenever he wished, and he was not going to be told by any member of parliament, either.
Some of you hecklers-and the champion heckler is among you-do not know about this. He means you and me, too. He means he is not going to be told by you, either. He is going to revoke it as and when he pleases. Why not revert to those old policies of the great old historic Liberal party, those policies the Liberal party has championed before the public at every election in the last quarter of a century, to trust the people and to trust parliament? Why not make parliament supreme again? Why hold parliament under suspicion?
If the minister and the cabinet believe there is an emergency, why not come before parliament and say, "We have agreed there is an emergency in Canada." If you want to call a private session, as I suggested the other day, then do so. Clear the galleries and have a private session of parliament behind closed doors and tell us about the emergency. We will not get frightened and run home for fear the parliament buildings will be blown up. We shall have to stay here if we are true to our obligations. Trust the house. I would even trust the back-benchers on the other side about whom I know very little except that I see them rise in humble submission and vote for everything that comes up. I expect they will even vote for this, though it will tie their hands in the future. We have not heard much from them in the past, and if this bill passes we will not hear much in the future.
Trust one man to invoke and revoke this measure; trust one man to invoke and revoke the rights of parliament. Is it possible that one man wants to be above parliament? I do not think that is in his mind. The Minister of Defence Production does not seem to like parliament. That is unfair for a man with his name.

That may sound to my hon. friend as abusing a privilege; it may sound far-fetched. It has been stated here on many occasions that freedom has fallen in other places. It has been nipped a little bit at times to get control of parliament. The methods may be fine, but so far as this country is concerned the methods are not the kind we should follow. They are at least mysterious.
As the minister said to us today, the purpose of the act is only to control materials. He said some companies are all right. He said some companies may say they are satisfied with the progress of our management. Remember, this government are supposed to be great company managers. If there is anything wrong with the textile industry it is not because of goods coming in from the outside. If there is anything wrong with the electrical business, it is not because of goods coming in from outside; it is because the executive does not know how to run it. Those past masters of industry know how to run it. I should like to see the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) run General Electric, or some of these other companies. If he did not run them any better than he runs his department they would go broke.

The Minister of Defence Production said today that the companies that are producing are using the taxpayers' money. It was rather refreshing to learn that the ministers at last are starting to worry about the taxpayers' money. A few years ago the cry was "What's a million?" Today they are beginning to be concerned about the taxpayers' money. It is the taxpayers' money we are spending. What did they think they were spending until now? They have been spending far more on civil administration than they ever spent before
Defence Production Act and far less on defence, even though defence is getting more important. The emergency is increasing and their expenditures are less. Even though the need for keeping down civil expenditures is greater, and inflation is increasing, they are still spending more. It is grand to find that they are now almost weeping crocodile tears about the poor taxpayers' money.
If they do not like the way a company is being run they want the power, as the minister said today, to go in and say, "You have been running your company for 25 years. I do not like the way you run it. I have never run a company like this myself but I think we down here in Ottawa, the cabinet, are able to run it better than you can. We have a lot of money invested here. We think differently from you, so just move over, move out. If you are not saucy about it, we can give you a good pension. We may give you a good pension anyway. Remember, if you are saucy about it we have an act. We do not need to give you anything. Step aside; let us in. We know how to run this." Does that mean that all departments are now going to be as permanently dictatorial as the Department of Defence Production, if these powers are made permanent?
The Minister of Defence Production said he could liquidate the act at any time, but would not be told by any member of the House of Commons when to do so. That means, if it means anything, that the minister says, "let us now invoke it; I will revoke it independently of parliament." He is in the twilight of his career, and when he retires we do not know who will take his place. I would not oppose that retirement myself, because I would like to see him remain in good health for the balance of his life.
The next normal step would be to have these powers exercised by some person else, but some other minister may be power-hungry. Such a minister might be ready to liquidate parliament altogether. You might just as well liquidate it as destroy its supremacy. You might just as well liquidate parliament as to refuse to trust parliament. You might just as well liquidate this house if you do not have full trust that the house will give the necessary powers in time of emergency.
In conclusion I say there is no hon. member within sound of my voice who would not give his or her life for this country. Despite our political differences, the cabinet know that at any time they have required power that power has not been refused. It would not be refused in the future in time of emergency. But we are being asked to


surrender the supremacy of parliament and place in the hands of one minister permanent powers of this kind.
I do not distrust the present Minister of Defence Production. I do not distrust him personally, as I have the highest regard for him. But principles are eternal, and we are fighting for principles. We do not propose to leave this house until we have fully expressed our convictions. We do not propose to leave this house even in the heat of this season until we feel we have done our duty. My hon. friends of the cabinet may smile, but I would remind some of the junior members who are here of a former champion of the supremacy of parliament. One of their great leaders told us how we should always trust the people. I can remember the late W. L. Mackenzie King standing out here in front of the mace and championing the supremacy of parliament.
I would refer hon. members to the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. But I know all hon. members opposite will again show that blind allegiance which is so conspicuous on their part. I am not surprised that some of them laugh, but I would remind them that he who laughs last laughs best. I would remind some of these great statesmen of what was said by those who were worshipped by their forefathers. I am not disturbed by all this noise, because I have learned long since that there is nothing less contributory to sound reason than empty laughter.
I thank the minister for giving me the attention he has. It is rather noticeable that the right hon. gentleman who moved the motion is not in attendance in the chamber and has not spoken during this debate, but the man who expects to get the power is waiting anxiously for it. I am glad that his socialist friends have stayed in the house with him, because I realize how all this will be written in the C.C.F. campaign books of the future, how the right hon. Minister of Defence Production put this into effect and set things up for the socialist state even though it was not a socialist who put it into effect. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the government supporters in this house show little interest in the dictatorial bill which the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) is bent on putting through, we of the official opposition find satisfaction in the thought that every sacrifice we make is gladly made for the defence and protection of the Canadian people and the safeguard of our democratic system.

As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) moved an amendment to this bill this afternoon, less than 30 Liberal members were in their seats in this house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: How many Conservative members are in the house just now? There are only four.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
That is about all the hon. member has said during this session, and it is not much of a contribution.
This should show how utterly indifferent they are to democracy or to the feelings of those they govern. Whatever criticism or suggestions we may offer are of no concern to them, nor is the fact that the most powerful of cabinet ministers is setting himself above parliament. They are by no means concerned with the interest of those whom they represent here, or with the constitution or respect for provincial rights. They are likewise completely indifferent to the democratic system under which we live and which allows them to sit in this house. The only thing that counts for our hon. friends, the Liberal members, is the exercise of power, for which they have a great fondness and which they hope to be able to retain for a long time to come. What a strange conception of duty that is, and how they will have to answer to the electorate for it!
At this time when this Canada of ours is more than ever in danger, when the shadows of war extend to our very doorstep, we are faced with the depressing and shameful sight of a government which mocks at the people and its defenders, a government which, armed with arbitrary powers, is rushing headlong into a socialism fraught with danger. This attitude can but lead us to the loss of our dearest freedoms, freedoms which we have, up to this moment, gained through courage, heroism and bloodshed.
History is there and one only has to read it to find out the heavy price that was paid for the freedom we now enjoy and which we want to preserve at any cost.
Let us go back to some ten years ago, and assess the sad cost of the five years of the second world war.
Let us pay a short visit to the various battlefields where those we must call our Canadian heroes fought gloriously. Let us recall for a moment the names of all those we knew and loved and who did not hesitate to answer the call of their country, who generously gave their lives for the preservation, in Canada and throughout the world, of the democratic system which has made our country what it is today.
Defence Production Act
Let us for a moment enter homes saddened by the loss of loved ones, losses caused by totalitarianism which wanted to deprive us of a freedom so dear to our hearts.
Why, Mr. Speaker, during the dark years of 1939-44, were we horrified witnesses of so many massacres, so much destruction and desolation, so many tears and so much bereavement? Why did our fine young men, Canadian youths, give or risk their lives away from their homes and the people they cherished? Why must thousands of them today lead a hapless existence, disabled or handicapped as a consequence of their war experience?
It is because they answered the call of those who were then the leaders of this country, the same who are sitting today at your right, Mr. Speaker, who dramatically and even with sobbing voices, were pressing and urging those young men, the hope and the future of the nation, to don the uniform, to take up arms and go overseas to protect the endangered freedom of this country.

The call to arms for the protection and defence of our democratic system was heard, and more than a million Canadians did not hesitate to answer the call of duty, trusting that because of their countless sacrifices, even the sacrifice of their lives, those who would come after them might completely enjoy the benefits of true democracy which is synonymous with peace, justice, happiness and prosperity.
Scarcely ten years have passed since thousandfold bereavement darkened our Canadian homes. Hardly a decade after the time when Canadians, all over the country, tightened their belts of their own free will, so that freedom and democracy might prevail, those who demanded the dread ransom are aping the dictators which democracy had overcome.
This bill is an encroachment on individual liberty, on the freedom of private enterprise and on the sacred rights of the provinces. It is one of the worst inroads ever made against the Canadian constitution in our whole history.
While we oppose with our utmost energy these dictatorial powers which would endanger our democratic system for the preservation of which so much blood has been shed, the Minister of Defence Production, showing a shocking contempt for the sacred document which is our constitution, contempt too for individuals and for the provinces and private enterprise generally, seems

Defence Production Act to repeat, looking at the sheepish majority around him, that sentence which should bring sad memories to him: "If we want to do it, who will stop us?"
Mr. Speaker, the minister was unable to convince us and he cannot convince the Canadian people that he needs such unlimited powers. They are unnecessary and he knows it.
Since hundreds of millions in taxpayers' money are spent each year by that department, the Canadian population which, through the high taxes it pays, is footing the bill wants to know and is entitled to know how that money is spent. Is that not the reason why every four or five years the government goes to the people so that 265 representatives are sent here to further and to protect the interests of the nation?
Never, under our parliamentary system has any government, tramping upon our most sacred rights, made such a servile use of the majority given to them to betray the electors, the very people who entrusted them with the management of our nation's business. Mr. Speaker, I state that the greatest part of the population, with the exception of a few communists and socialists, refuses to give the government this blank cheque. If the minister does get this blank cheque through the majority of those who like to show that they have become ambitious socialists, subservient to rigid party discipline, I suggest that such behaviour is a betrayal of the people, and that in due course the people will remember it.
Let us never forget this old saying which applies so well at this time to those who are making themselves the accomplices of the Minister of Defence Production, and are ready to grant him the dictatorial powers he demands: "You can fool some of the people some of the time, but you can't fool all the people all the time". Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has just interrupted finds it a laughing matter when a member of this house shows some respect for those who have elected him. If I have the pleasure and the honour of sitting in the parliament of my country it is because the electors of Quebec West have asked me to come here to fight for the great democratic principles which have made Canada what she is today, and they want us to pass on that heritage to those who will come after us.
If the present behaviour of the hon. member for Russell is all the heritage he will pass on to his electors and his people, I would say it is a very poor heritage, a very insignificant heritage, a very indifferent, a very -I will not use that other word, because it would be unparliamentary.
Mr. Speaker, a government cannot forever go on laughing at the people and deceiving them with impunity. Once again, the Liberal party, of which the hon. member for Russell

is a distinguished representative, has gone too far, and the next appeal to the people will show them what those who laugh at the people must expect.
In trying to gain by putting parliament to death the minister will only succeed in driving the last nail into the coffin of his political party.
I challenge each and every Liberal member in this house to be here when the question will be put with regard to this bill. I cannot for the life of me believe that without a single dissenting voice they will agree to lament over the loss of our democratic freedom.
People of Canada, your freedom is in jeopardy! People of Canada, the democracy you have so dearly bought in the past is dying, and is to be buried in a Liberal shroud! It is still time, however, to check that shameful dictatorship which is already trying to strangle us. We are too proud of our past and of our history not to ward off this slur.
Like the gallant warriors of old, let us stand together and say to the minister and to the government: "Hold, you shall not pass!"
And as we are heroically fighting for the defence of the democratic rights so dearly paid for, let us unite and preserve at least what freedoms are left to us.
I repeat the plea I made last week to all hon. members from my own province and to all French-speaking members, with the exception of the hon. member for Russell, because he has never known what it is all about and he won't understand any better tonight, and I say to them: We in French Canada have a glorious past, traditions which are dear to us and were preserved through the resistance of our fathers whose memory stirs our hearts. If we survived and grew into a great people which widely contributed to the development and progress of our Canadian country, it was because we had faith in freedom and democracy. Let us never defile a whole past of glory and the memory of those who were responsible for what we are today.
Wave aside partisanship, in this momentous and crucial hour, and rally around those who want to bequeath to future generations a Canada wherein they will still be in a position to breathe the unsullied air of liberty and democracy.
Let us generously join our English-speaking fellow citizens who, on this side of the house, want, as we do, to hand down to their descendants something better than an infamous dictatorship.
Be Liberals if you like, but be Liberals mainly in preserving for Canadians a country
Defence Production Act which will continue to be free and truly democratic!
I do repeat, Mr. Speaker, that more than ever the time has come for our friends opposite to give up party politics and to think at least once in their lifetime of our Canadian fatherland.

The change the government is making by this bill has turned it into a real issue, Mr. Speaker. It strikes at parliament's very existence and places it in jeopardy. The deletion of the time limit by the government is serious enough. What is more serious is the thinking of the government, or the thinking behind the idea that they could get away with this. By presenting it as merely an innocuous measure to expedite defence production, as it stands now it is bidding for power in perpetuity. What confronts us now is this attempt, whether wittingly or unwittingly, to undermine the very base upon which the principles of our democracy are founded.
Section 5 of the act confirms this, because it says:
The minister may authorize any person, on his behalf or under his control and direction, to do any act or thing or to exercise any power that the minister may do or exercise under this act.
Did Hitler, Mussolini, Stalin or Peron ask for any greater power? Why, absolute mon-archs never exercised so much, nor tried to exercise it. Then, Mr. Speaker, we would be recreant to our sworn fealty to the crown, to the people of this great dominion, if we did not oppose this bill to the full extent of our ability.
Why, Mr. Speaker, we are performing an outstanding service to the people of Canada by whom we have been encouraged and supported through the press, by organizations and individuals to challenge the government and to continue our opposition to the utmost limit before granting such complete power; and any delay in the adoption of this bill, no matter how brief, gives that much longer to enjoy the freedom that is being filched from us, and drive home with greater impact the government's depredation of their rights.
We have seen these things in the past. History is replete with lessons of how power was innocently given, with no intention of being taken advantage of or being abused, only to see the people and the nation humbled and the initiators, the creators, yes, the perpetrators of the use of the power pursue their course into oblivion by devious means. Does not the government by now realize that the power this bill gives to the minister and his successors, regardless of who they may

Defence Production Act be and irrespective of party affiliation, is dangerous and fraught with far-reaching and undemocratic features never before presented in peacetime?
Why, Mr. Speaker, the power the minister and his successors seek is to compel Canadian industry to accept government contracts or orders at what he considers the right price, under threat of seizure of their plants. This is a power that has no place in our democratic system at any time.
Should anyone harbour in his mind any doubt that this power now being asked for will be used, let me dispel that. The Minister of Defence Production presents his own case, with ample evidence, that he will run things his own way without parliament's help or advice. He emphasized his contempt for parliament when he stated, "If we have overstepped our powers, I make no apology for having done so"; also his cavalier manner when talking of the people's money, "What's a million?"; and again when he handled this house like a martinet and told the members, "Who will stop us?"
Having had such despotic powers over the nation's economy for so long, he now wants to extend them indefinitely; a perfect example of how power feeds upon power and now finds that it cannot survive without it and will not relinquish it. At the present time he wonders who is going to stop him. The battle is joined, and we shall carry on in defence of that principle. He did not use the exact expression of General Grant when he was talking about General Lee and the Battle of the Wilderness, and said he would fight this out if it took all summer. That is the attitude he has taken, and for a man who is generally very reasonable, it is hard to understand his obstinacy in this matter.

While we are aware that both business and labour have their bad actors, whom no one attempts to condone, by and large both industry and labour were patriotic and gave their best. Both did moderately well. In fact labour came at last to the uplands of better times, and they are still advancing. What with government checks and balances, restraints, verbotens and permits, inspectors' investigations, collectors, controllers, comptrollers, directors and deputies and ministers; with their graded scales and schedules, lists and levies, imposts, taxes and tariffs, how anyone could enter into the Elysian field of large profits without the consent of some of the mentioned individuals is beyond comprehension. We could not expect anything better from the other side, but we are tolerant and can submit to such things. Down through the history of this country from its very start, not just from confederation; down through British history, we And incidents such as this; of charters of freedom which have taken years to secure being ignored and superseded by just some such insignificant act as this. Step by step, instead of retaining the liberties they had gained in the past they found them gradually withdrawn one after another because like so many countries which have gone by the way and are not now in existence, they ignored, or allowed someone to delude them by granting, some innocuous piece of legislation that was going to do them good. Someone was going to govern better than they could govern themselves. In other words they were too stupid to be governed by themselves and therefore they must be given direction.
They returned to the old oriental philosophy of the Pharaohs, of Genghis Khan and those who wanted absolute power. They were told that no harm would be done; that if they obeyed orders they would be handsomely taken care of. That has been the basis of legislation such as this that we are dealing with today.
You may think we are wasting time here tonight in presenting this opposition. We do not consider we are. Hitler thought he was going on for a thousand years and said so. Other dictators said the millennium had come and would continue. With such a bill as this the people may realize some day that that which they cherished most highly has been taken away from them.
The Minister of Defence Production advanced what he considered were reasons for this bill by stating that certain metals such as nickel were scarce and were needed for defence purposes. What about gold and silver? The government now have the means of controlling those metals any time they desire. There is no necessity for a bill of this kind. The government can put on an embargo or put on controls any time they see fit. That is no excuse for bringing down a bill such as this. The minister has never failed in the past to acquire the powers he wanted when and how he wanted them, if needed.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the minds of some hon. members this skirmish is assuming the proportions of a major battle. I agree that it is the last engagement in a running encounter which has gone on since 1945 over a principle which is certainly worth fighting for. The principle for which we have been fighting and in which all Conservatives believe, and I think not a few Liberals, may be described as the belief that the discretion allowed to men in power must be reduced to the lowest level consistent with the effective operation of the political machinery. "Men in power", in the context of this debate and in the application of this bill to the situation in Canada, is not limited to the minister or his successor but includes those officials in his department to whom he has the power to delegate authority, and to the agents, investigators, controllers and others outside the public service altogether to whom the minister may redelegate the very broad authorities given to him by this bill.
If the Minister of Defence Production, who appears to have taken the ministerial responsibility for this bill apart from the formal approval given by the Prime Minister, in whose name the bill stands, were somewhat more conciliatory in his make-up the amendment the house now has before it would seem to offer a reasonable compromise between the opposing forces, which at this stage of the discussion appear to be represented by a determination on the part of the minister to write his broad powers into the permanent law of Canada, on the one hand, and the determination of the opposition to resist any such attempt and not to yield until they are overwhelmed by the weight of numbers on the other hand.
The minister reviewed the history of the procurement of defence supplies during the last 16 years, that is since the outbreak of world war II. It might be appropriate to review the counterbalancing powers which were given and which were used during that period in connection with the procurement of those supplies. It began, of course, with the outbreak of world war II. For the next five years, that is until 1945, there was no protest in this house against the delegation of the most extensive powers that any government in this country had ever been given by parliament.
Those powers were broadened and strengthened as the experience of the war dictated, and when hostilities ceased a fairly broad code had been formulated by the minister and the departmental officials which covered almost any conceivable action the government needed to take in the stress of a total war effort.

Defence Production Act
The next stage in this history was after the cessation of hostilities, when battle was joined over the continuation of the war measures powers under the emergency powers act, which granted powers based on the continuation of a state of emergency, as the name implies. That act, which replaced the War Measures Act, continued in effect for several years and was modified from time to time in the course of this engagement which, as I described, is continuing tonight over precisely the same issue.
In the course of those engagements the emergency powers act was modified, and eventually the government appeared to be persuaded that the emergency powers were no longer needed, for they allowed the bill to lapse entirely, I believe three years ago. That pretty well disposed of powers based on the theory that there was an emergency. We have on the statute books only this bill. This bill, whilst it is objectionable, having a very broad delegation of powers for a peacetime government or at least a government which is not engaged in active hostilities, nevertheless is somewhat more restricted than the emergency powers bill. Those somewhat more restricted powers had been enacted by this parliament in 1951 with a definite time limit which is to be reached next year, on the 31st July, 1956.
So when the government appeared to accept the proposition over which this running engagement had taken place-that is the proposition that the powers dependent on the state of emergency were no longer needed- we had nothing left but a bill which was due to expire at a fixed time and which had not yet expired. At least its objectionable features were largely offset by the fact that its expiration was expected.
There was, of course, the other bill to which the minister has referred, the defence supplies act, which is suspended while the Defence Production Act is in force but would come into force again if the Defence Production Act were repealed. At this point in this long controversy we have before us a bill which is not due to expire until another 13 months have elapsed. In other words there will be another session of this parliament before it is necessary finally to deal with the powers aspect of the bill.
I appreciate, and everyone who has spoken from this side appreciates, that it is necessary to make a decision about the Department of Defence Production. It has been generally agreed that the department is necessary and should be continued, and that this can be done without the powers which the minister
[Mr. Michener.l

claims to be necessary. If that course were taken this matter would be resolved very quickly.
The amendment we have before us suggests a very reasonable way of bringing together the forces which appear to be locked in disagreement at the present time, those forces I have already described. This amendment simply would refer the bill and the principle of continuing the department to the standing committee on banking and commerce, a committee on which the government has a very large majority and which is presided over by one of its distinguished supporters. If the bill were sent to that committee it could consider the need for the powers; it could sort out the powers in the bill, consider which are necessary and which are unnecessary, and rewrite the bill or make recommendations which would be acceptable to the committee and presumably to the house, at the same time dealing with the problem of putting the Department of Defence Production on a permanent basis.
To my mind that seems a reasonable proposition which could readily be accepted by this house in view of the time element, in view of the seriousness of the controversy which has existed over this last 10 years on the subject of emergency powers, and in view of the present deadlock on this issue.
It perhaps would be easier to follow the government in its decision not to accept some middle ground if a better case had been made for the powers to which objection has been taken. They surely must be justified on the basis of some serious need. No one on this side, at least, has been persuaded by the attempts which have been made-and I am sure in fairness the government will agree no very serious attempt has been made-to present a case which would justify the full extent of the powers which were written into this bill at a time when Canada was engaged in open warfare in Korea.
I speak with more confidence on this subject because the only attempts which have been made so far have been those of the minister himself and one or two of his colleagues. I recall at least one of the private members on the government side, the hon. member for Spadina. Some of his arguments were based on such erroneous grounds that they rather shattered the whole case he intended to make, a case which has been described today by several members as not in conformity with his usual liberal viewpoint on public affairs. I refer to his argument which appears on page 5006 of Hansard, wherein he suggests why it is necessary for us to continue these powers in force. He is

following the Leader of the Opposition and trying to make a case by example. He says:
Let me give you some examples, as the Leader of the Opposition gave you some examples. Let us take the field of electronics, a very important field. Many important and essential patents are now in use. We need them. If we do not have them, they can well retard our defence effort and in some cases nullify it.
Is there anyone who will say we do not need the power to take and use these patents and to compensate people for them?
That sounds like a reasonable proposition, but when one looks at the powers the government has already under the Patent Act it is quite clear that the government needs nothing further. I refer to the Patent Act in the Revised Statutes of Canada. Section 22 reads as follows:
Any patent application for an invention that, in the opinion of the commissioner, relates to the production, application or use of atomic energy-
And so on. That is not the section I had in mind. It is section 19 of the act, which reads:
The government of Canada may, at any time, use any patented invention, paying to the patentee such sum as the commissioner reports to be a reasonable compensation for the use thereof, and any decision of the commissioner under this section is subject to appeal to the exchequer court.
That is one provision which the hon. member has obviously overlooked, and it lets down a very important part of the case he endeavoured to make in support of these powers. If you look further through what he said there is nothing which indicates a need for the extensive powers which we are asked to approve today.
That is one attempt that was made. The minister himself made quite an extensive argument in favour of the continuation of these powers in the light of his own experience and belief, and we must give him credit for sticking to his guns and insisting that he needs these powers. But what does he say is the reason he needs them? The first point I wish to deal with is that he says this department, like other departments, has to have its powers and this act has to be taken as a unit because in it you have the constitution of the department as well as the powers and authority which the department must exercise. Therefore he says if we reject the powers we reject the department. He refers to other departments of government, public works and finance, in illustration of how a department is established.
I have taken the trouble to look at the statutes establishing these departments. The Public Works Act, which is chapter 228 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, establishes the Department of Public Works. I submit that the minister was probably picking the best examples he could. The Department of
Defence Production Act Public Works is a department which has the power to take from any citizen of Canada any real estate, any real property, which it needs to expropriate for purposes of the government, and to compensate for that expropriation. But when you look at the way the department is established you find that the act says very little about expropriation. The powers of expropriation are contained in quite another act of parliament, in another volume of the Revised Statutes of Canada. They are found in the Expropriation Act.
The department's statute simply establishes the department, names a minister and defines his authority in general terms. "Department" is defined as meaning the department of the government of Canada charged with the construction and maintenance of public works, and a minister is named to take charge of it. Therefore the parallel is clear now that what should be done to establish a new and permanent department of government under the name of defence production is to pass a general bill setting up the department, naming a minister and giving it the basic authority.

Defence Production Act to say it will go on until some reason reappears among those who call themselves Liberals.
Let us see what else the minister produced by way of argument in support of the need for these powers. He went on to deal with the question of scarcity and the need for rationing. His first example was nickel. Canada, producing as it does approximately 95 per cent of the world's nickel, is in a pretty good position to have the nickel it needs, and the minister does not complain that we are not getting what nickel is needed for defence purposes. The government, far from undertaking to develop more nickel on its own initiative, has allowed the government of the United States to do that in a rather unusual way, by writing individual contracts with the large nickel producers so there is no uniform price for nickel.
The great producers of nickel, the International Nickel Company Limited and Falcon-bridge Nickel Mines, both have their private engagements with the United States government by which means that government procures a very large percentage of the production of those two major nickel mines. This does not establish a uniform price, and other producers may not find a ready means of obtaining the same advantage. That is not an issue tonight, but that is the situation in the nickel industry. There seems to be no concern on the part of the government about establishing a price, and as the minister himself said the nickel producers were not tempted by the higher price abroad to withhold any part of their production.
The minister mentioned copper. He also mentioned steel for the early warning lines. If the minister had taken steps recently to foster the steel industry in this country and increase our production at least to the point where we were self-sustaining instead of allowing our iron ore to be taken abroad to be smelted, perhaps there would be some point in what he says; but as long as the government is no more concerned about the supply of iron and steel in this country than they are at present it does not seem to me that a very good case has been made for the use of these great powers in order to get what steel is needed for the early warning lines.
The minister said these instances illustrate the possibility of the need for rationing. The minister does not seriously tell the house we are in need of rationing of scarce materials today. On the contrary, the minister and his department voluntarily abandoned all rationing. I stand to be corrected if I am not right, but my impression is there is no rationing of scarce materials in Canada today and no need for any.
