speechtext: There has not been for several years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
There has not been for a couple of years. Therefore that part of the minister's case does not have much persuasive force. The only serious case he attempted to make was related to some major projects of the defence program. They were the development of supersonic aircraft and engines, which I submit is almost entirely under the control of the government in the ordinary course of events by its contracts and its financial support. These are not the natural industries of this country. We would not have them if the government were not developing these aircraft and engines. Therefore it is a matter of the government being in the business already, and it needs no powers to deal with a business it runs itself. The powers the minister has here would enable him to deal with any kind of industry throughout the whole country, whereas his case is limited to industry which is already within the government's own control.
The same applies to the other major projects he mentioned, the naval gun and the early warning and guided missile projects. They are all armament projects and are in their nature very closely controlled and entirely financed by the government itself. Surely no case is made for a general, broad control of industry by citing such examples as those. After all, the materials which go into these items are not the whole range of industrial supplies; and if the minister rests on that I submit it is a completely inadequate case to persuade any reasonable parliament that these powers, extraordinary as they are, should be continued in a time of peace.
In his justification of this bill today the minister goes on to say that no question of freedom is involved. Let us look at that. It is admitted that the bill does not give the power to suspend habeas corpus, to seize the person of anyone engaged in industry and throw him into jail except after a trial. There is no difference of opinion on that score, therefore. But to say that no question of freedom of the individual is involved to my mind overlooks the whole basis and concept of freedom which depends, in its essence, upon there being people who are not slaves in any economic sense of the word, able to express themselves without fear of retaliation. In that sense there is no question in my mind but that the freedom and liberty of the individual is involved.
The liberty of the individual comprises all his normal rights of property as well as freedom from arrest. Property is an important right of an individual, as any lawyer can

tell you, because two-thirds of the concerns of his clients are in the defence of their property rights. If a man who is running a business is subject to having that business taken over by arbitrary action-because it is within the discretion of the minister that such action can be taken-to me that indicates there is a potential interference with the liberty of the individual which the minister has entirely overlooked or disregarded.
If you look for a minute at the possible effect on a man's business and property of the exercise of the powers which are in existence under this act, I think everyone in this house will agree that the potentiality is there. No one is saying that it has been exercised or that it will necessarily be exercised. But as long as the potentiality is there it is a threat to the liberty and freedom of the subject. As I interpret section 27, and I think this is the right interpretation of it, where the minister is satisfied that a person who has taken a defence contract is likely to fail to perform that contract in a businesslike manner, the minister may authorize a controller to carry on the whole of the business of that person. Is that not a ferocious weapon to put in the hands of anyone for the purpose of getting someone to carry out a defence contract in a businesslike manner?
The minister has very properly given high praise to Canadian industry for carrying out its contracts in a businesslike and efficient manner. The only instance he cited where he felt the need for authority to intervene and appoint a better management was in connection with a project directly under the control of the government. In so far as industry generally is concerned, you will find that the interests of the government and of business coincide. They are both out to do business and have it done in an efficient and businesslike manner. This power the minister has depends on his being satisfied that such and such is not the case. In other words it depends simply on his being dissatisfied with the way a man is running some part of his business. Then he can put in a controller to operate the whole of that man's business. If this would not be an unwarranted interference with a man's liberty I should like to know what this house means by "liberty".
Actually the controller who may be put in under those circumstances is made the agent for the owner. Regardless of that owner's consent he has the power to commit the owner to all kinds of contracts and obligations which may not turn out well. In the end they may very well ruin the business completely. So far as I know-and perhaps the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who
Defence Production Act is also a lawyer, might verify this-the only case of compulsory agency in the law is that of one's wife, and that is limited to the purchase of necessities. Here we have a case of compulsory agency where there is no limitation in the act at all. That is the kind of interference with property rights that is written into this bill.
Then the next section deals with relief from obligation. I am not going to take time to go into that, but the amazing thing about it is that the minister alone, if I am not mistaken, has the power to relieve a man from statutory obligation under an act passed by this parliament. That goes about as far as any legislation can go.
These powers are supplemented by the power to investigate. We all know what a weighty power the power to investigate can be. It is a very common practice with governments to give broad powers of investigation, to send investigators in without even a signature to look through a man's affairs and find whatever they can to convict him of whatever they want. This power of investigation, combined with the power of control and the power of relief from other statutory obligations, is in effect the power to ruin a person engaged in business. It is the power to intimidate business. So long as these powers exist the way they are, potentially they are powers of intimidation which form a cloud on the freedom of business and industry generally throughout this country.
Under those circumstances, if the minister comes into this house and says there is no interference with liberty, I suggest he is not looking the facts in the face. He is not giving this house a true impression of what those powers are. It would be more commendable on his part if he were to say yes, we are going to interfere with the liberty of the subject in the exercise of his broad rights with respect to his and other people's property, but it is necessary for these reasons. Then he could give his reasons.
I have gone over all the reasons he gave, except the final one. The final reason is, I believe, insulting to the intelligence of the house. He said there is nothing new in these powers; they have existed for 16 years, and therefore they are all right. You do not have to examine that proposition very far to see what an absurdity it is. It is simply an assertion that conditions have not changed very much. We all know what kind of conditions existed from 1939 to 1945 and the powers which were necessary to carry on a totalitarian conflict which has been renewed sporadically and which still threatens to break out. But at least we can define our present

With that, Mr. Speaker, I submit again that this bill has not been supported by any rational arguments. Mr. Speaker, in commencing my second speech on this important question I find myself in a much happier situation than I was two weeks ago last night. When we began this debate we had a somewhat lonely feeling. We knew what the attitude of the rest of the House of Commons was, and we were assured that this was a trivial matter that no sane man outside the House of Commons would pay any attention to. We had to pull ourselves together and make ourselves believe that, in spite of being a rather small number, we possibly could be right.
Two weeks have elapsed since then, and we do not feel quite so lonely as we did. I must admit that at that time there was some reason for the feeling some people had. I remember that one of our friends who, I think, is a good political forecaster said, when this thing came up, "Don't let us fool ourselves. If we take this thing on, at first there will be no interest in it at all. The press will not be interested. Nobody will be interested. But if we fight it through and make people believe we really do regard it as a matter of principle on which we are prepared to take some trouble, then people will become interested in spite of themselves".
I have some rather interesting proof of that. Two or three weeks ago, after this debate began, one of my journalist friends whom I greatly respect was having a meal with me, and I said, "You don't seem to have any interest in this matter in your newspaper. You have not had an editorial. Your report yesterday did not suggest there was even a glimmering of any principle involved." He said, "Are you people serious about this?" I said, "Yes, we are. You can take it from me that we are."

We are serious; and I think if this has to go on people will realize in a week or two-or more-from now that we are more serious even than they realize at the moment.
I do not wish to say this in any pious way, but I think we have a duty to carry this to the people of Canada, and to public opinion; and we are trying to do it.
It is possible to turn back a government. It does not happen often, but it did happen once in this house since I have been here. It was a rather small matter having to do with tendering for public works, and the amount of a contract in respect of which tenders must be called. But for some reason-perhaps because the opposition were able to express themselves a little more forcibly-whatever the reason was, we got across to the press. We broke through to the press in a rather big way, as a matter of fact. In two weeks' time public opinion had asserted itself and that bill had to be changed.
In the present instance we have not done that, in the two weeks it has taken, and the government has not backed down. As I say, at the moment we have to comfort ourselves with the fact that we have been doing our manifest duty. We take some comfort from the fact that it is getting across in the country, and some of the best newspapers are taking hold of it. While I do not flatter myself that the man in the street has got hold of it yet, I do believe if the newspapers will take hold of it, and keep hold of it, they will be able to make the public take enough time off from less important things to realize just what this means. I was staggered, consternated, to find that my high-class journalist friend had not taken an interest in it. But I will say this, that once he believed we were serious he began to take an interest in it mighty fast, and he has been showing a great deal of interest in it ever since.

And so I say that in two weeks two things have happened. First of all, the press has begun to take hold. Indeed, it has begun in a rather big way. I hope the minister read the editorial the other day in the Winnipeg Free Press entitled "Drop this Bill", because it was a powerful editorial, and I should not think he could read it with comfort. Then one or two other newspapers, notably the Calgary Herald, warmed my heart because they perceived the principle we see, and they spoke about it in words that were encouraging.
I propose to refer to some editorial comments. Before doing that, however, I shall refer not to an editorial but to a cartoon which appeared in the Montreal Gazette yesterday. In this cartoon the minister is depicted as a very effective looking baseball player. I do not know if he did play baseball, but he is depicted here in that way. He has hold of a huge bat, about three times as long as himself, which he is holding lightly in one hand. The bat is labelled "Defence powers with no time limit." Then there is a poor, miserable little character labelled "parliament", who is standing before the minister, looking up at him with a terrified aspect. I think it is the pitcher; he does not wear a mask, although he does wear glasses, and I think that would be the pitcher. The ball is lying beside the plate. It would seem that the minister must have missed the last pitch. The minister is saying to this poor, little, miserable creature, who stands looking at him aghast, "I get all the strikes I want".
That seems to me to put it rather well. That is the way I feel about it. I was going to say that for some reason I cannot understand-and yet I think I do understand-I believe this is a personal matter, one in which the minister's personal feelings have become involved. I can well imagine that an all-powerful minister might feel lonely if he were deprived of these powers when, as he told us today, he has had them for 16 years with only a small break. I have no doubt it is a very upsetting thing to feel that he might not have them any longer.
I have spoken about the press, and I realize the rules do not permit my quoting. -Do we want a minister, a representative of the people, to exercise essential powers in an emergency, or are we prepared to leave those essential powers to be exercised by the great industrialists of this country, no matter how well intentioned they are? Let me give you some examples, as the Leader of the Opposition gave you some examples. Let us take the field of electronics, a very important field. Many important and essential patents are now in use. We need them. If we do not have them, they can well retard our defence effort and in some cases nullify it.
He was implying that co-operation in the electronics field was not forthcoming.
Is there anyone who will say we do not need the power to take and use these patents and to compensate people for them? We may be needing supplies such as strategic materials which are unavailable to us in the ordinary course of business. Is there anyone who will say that we should not have the right to take and use those strategic materials and to compensate those people?
In other words he was implying that the people in the electronics field were not willing to co-operate with the government in providing them with the materials and the information they need. Now I want to quote from what the hon. member for Ottawa West said, and after that I should like to quote from the report of the Department of Defence Production for last year, to show you what this report says regarding the willingness of people in that field to co-operate and the results that have been achieved. The hon. member for Ottawa West said, and I quote

his words from the top of the righthand column of page 5015 of Hansard:
Now there is such a mass of electronic equipment involved that certainly any limited comprehension I have of a technical subject like that is strained to understand even the most elementary things about such equipment. It takes a matter of three years to procure some articles. The field of radar is one in which Canadians can take very great pride, for the Canadian effort in radar has been not inconsiderable. When you examine into some of the electronic devices and what is required to produce them, you realize that, after an emergency arises or a war begins, it is not just a matter of going out and buying them; it is a matter of intensive effort three or four years preceding the time that equipment is required.
Then when you deal with the procurement of aircraft and examine into the type of metals required, you find a degree of quality required in those metals that was not thought of even in 1951, when this bill was previously up for discussion. Those types of metals are neither developed nor produced; nor are the other engineering problems involved in putting them into the finished article worked out after an outbreak of war, if that equipment is to be of any use in any such war.
That again implies there has been a great deal of difficulty in obtaining equipment and supplies, particularly in the field of electronics. I contend there has been no difficulty whatsoever, that industry of all kinds has been extremely co-operative as far as the government is concerned in producing equipment, producing information and giving every co-operation. To prove that I should like to quote from page 21 of the report of the Department of Defence Production for 1954. Under the heading "Electronics Branch" there is the following:
The production of electronic equipment for the Canadian armed forces continued during 1954 at the high level reached in the preceding year.
Note that. It did not merely proceed at a normal level but at a high level.
Canadian ability to produce the wide range of electronic items required for the defence program increased during the year with the result that a greater portion of components and end items was manufactured in this country. Of particular importance was the fact that Canada's productive capacity in this field has been built up mainly by private investment. A small amount of capital assistance was provided by the government for the creation and expansion of electronic facilities.
In other words the industry went ahead with the job by themselves and were completely co-operative. The report goes on to say:
Electronic equipment for Canada's fighter and trainer aircraft continued to be delivered on schedule.
There was no hold-up there. There was no need for these wide powers. The equipment was delivered on schedule. Electronic equipment was produced at a high level. Where was the hold-up? Where is the need for these excessive powers? There is none. From the

government's own report it is apparent that everything was produced on time and at a high level. I continue:
These items have included Canadian-produced gunfire control radars, radio compasses, aircraft radio identification and recognition equipment and automatic pilots. The initial requirement for a very high frequency (VHF) airborne communications equipment was completed during the year.
There is nothing here about any hold-back. No delays are mentioned.
Deliveries of flight simulators for the F-86 (Sabre) commenced late in the year, and production in Canada of flight simulators for the CF-100 (Canuck) was begun. Production of support items and spares for the Royal Canadian Air Force throughout the year included ground control approach systems, diesel generator sets, various types of ground transmitters and receivers, navigational aid installations and mobile microwave units.
Requirements of the Royal Canadian Navy were met with the delivery of such items as gunfire control systems, anti-submarine mortar mounting and control systems and automatic degaussing equipment.
Everything was delivered on time. There are no complaints about any delays. Nobody needed to be urged. Industry came through on time. Where is the need for all these powers to require industry to produce faster and better? There is no evidence of it in the department's own report. The report continues:
Canadian army requirements for proximity fuses for projectiles, radar gunfire control apparatus and a great variety of radio and line communication equipment continued to be met. .	.	. Repair,
overhaul and maintenance work increased in 1954 as a result of the continuing high level of equipment deliveries to the armed forces.
There were no hold-ups there at all. Why do we need these extraordinary powers? I continue:
Nearly all of this work was done in Canada. Development work on a number of important electronic projects continued during the year. These included electronic equipment for airborne guided missiles, mobile and shipboard radars, and many types of electronic instruments. .	.	.
Deliveries and installations for the first line of the continental radar defence system were completed in the earlier part of the year. The second line, that of the mid-Canada early warning system, reached the detailed planning and organizational stage by late 1954.
There is no evidence whatsoever of any hold-ups in the government's own report on defence production for last year. The minister tells us he has to have
Defence Production Act special powers, tremendous, comprehensive, overriding powers, to force industry to produce on time. According to the government's own report, industry has produced on time. This business of needing these extra powers is a lot of nonsense and the minister knows it from his own report. His department has said that every order placed has either been produced on time or ahead of schedule. A high level of production of all materials was maintained throughout the year.

I saw the Speaker was not rising to answer. What I have said is completely different from what I said before. May I call it ten o'clock now and move the adjournment of the debate?
On motion of Mr. Hees the debate was adjourned.

Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

Then we will take the motion to go into supply and if we achieve supply we will take the estimates of justice and veterans affairs.
